sets.q1: Listing or rule: how do you give a set?
sets.q2: Subset or element: what is the difference between ⊆ and ∈?
sets.q3: Intersection, union, difference: which part is which?
sets.q4: De Morgan: what is the opposite of an intersection?
sets.q5: How many go to at least one club? The sieve
sets.q6: Are there as many even numbers as whole numbers?
sets.defineIntro: Picture a box you put things into: here you choose from twelve numbered shapes. There are two ways to say what is in the box — list the elements, or give a rule and let in everything the rule fits. Click the elements and watch when one of the ready-made rules describes your selection too.
sets.defineDef1: Set: a collection of things where, for any thing, it is unambiguous whether it belongs; the things that belong are its elements (x ∈ A).
sets.defineDef2: Giving a set: either by listing — naming its elements — or by a rule: state a property, and everything satisfying it belongs.
sets.defineRuleLabel: Given by a rule, the same set:
sets.defineResult: The same set of {{size}} elements given two ways: the listing and the rule pick out exactly the same elements.
sets.defineResultNone: No ready-made rule fits this selection, so it can only be given by listing — it is still a set, with {{size}} elements.
sets.defineTask: Click the elements for which this holds: divisible by 3 and greater than 6.
sets.defineHint: Both conditions must hold at once, so 3 and 6 do not qualify.
sets.relIntro: The number 6 is an element of the set of even numbers: 6 ∈ A. The set of multiples of 6 is not an element but a subset: every one of its elements lies in A. So ∈ links an element to a set, while ⊆ links two sets. Pick two rules and see which relation comes out.
sets.relDef: Subset: A is a subset of B (A ⊆ B) if every element of A is also an element of B. If B also has an element that A lacks, then A is a proper subset of B (A ⊂ B).
sets.rel_equal: A = B — the sets are equal, holding exactly the same elements.
sets.rel_subsetAB: A ⊆ B — every element of A is in B, but B has an element that A does not.
sets.rel_subsetBA: B ⊆ A — every element of B is in A, but A has an element that B does not.
sets.rel_disjoint: A ∩ B = ∅ — the sets are disjoint, sharing no element.
sets.rel_overlap: They share elements, but neither is a subset of the other.
sets.relTask: Set the two rules so that A is a proper subset of B: every element of A lies in B, and the two are not equal.
sets.relHint: Look for a property stricter than another. Whatever is divisible by 6 is also even.
sets.opsIntro: Two or three circles cut the universe into regions: each region says which circles you are inside and which you are outside. Pick an expression, or switch on free drawing, shade whatever you like, and see what the result is called.
sets.opsDef1: Union (A ∪ B): what lies in A or in B — one of them is enough.
sets.opsDef2: Intersection (A ∩ B): what lies in A and in B as well.
sets.opsDef3: Difference (A ∖ B): what lies in A but not in B.
sets.opsDef4: Complement (Ā): the part of the universal set that falls outside A.
sets.opsNoName: This shading has no simple name among the ones listed. Every set of regions can be described, but not all of them have a short form.
sets.opsTask: Shade the region this expression denotes. Click the diagram or use the buttons.
sets.opsHint: Shade only what lies in A but in neither B nor C.
sets.dmIntro: "I have an umbrella and a cap." When is that false? Not only when you have neither — one of them missing is enough. Sets work the same way: the complement of A ∩ B is not Ā ∩ B̄. Switch between the two laws and compare the left and right drawings.
sets.dmAria_inter_left: Venn diagram: complement of A intersect B
sets.dmAria_inter_right: Venn diagram: union of the complements of A and B
sets.dmAria_union_left: Venn diagram: the complement of the union of A and B
sets.dmAria_union_right: Venn diagram: the intersection of the complement of A and the complement of B
sets.dmSame: The two shadings are identical: the left and the right side cover exactly the same regions.
sets.dmNote: De Morgan’s two laws: negating an intersection gives the union of the negations, and negating a union gives their intersection. So negation always swaps “and” for “or”, and the other way round.
sets.dmTask: Which expression describes the shaded region?
sets.dmHint: It is the shared part that is left out. That makes it the complement of the intersection.
sets.dmRegionsHint: The shading covers {{regions}} of the four regions.
sets.countIntro: In a class 18 go to football, 15 to swimming and 7 to both. Add 18 and 15 and you have counted those 7 people twice. Retype the region sizes, drag the slider and watch the × marks: when the sieve finishes, every region must read exactly ×1.
sets.countStep0: Start from nothing. Drag the slider right and the sieve builds up one step at a time.
sets.countStepMid: Look at the × marks: overlapping regions have now been counted more than once. The next step corrects that.
sets.countStepDone: Every region reads ×1. That is exactly why the sieve works: after the alternating sum, each element has been counted precisely once.
sets.countTask: A class has {{all}} students. Of them {{foot}} play football, {{swim}} swim, and {{both}} do both. How many do neither?
sets.countHint: First work out how many do at least one sport, then subtract from the class size.
sets.infIntro: In a class of ten there are certainly fewer girls than ten: for a finite set a proper subset is smaller. For infinite sets that breaks down — every positive integer has exactly one even partner, and the other way round. Drag the slider and see whether anyone is left unpaired.
sets.infParadox: The even numbers form a proper subset of the positive integers, and yet there are exactly as many of them. Switch on the true number line: the arrows fan out and the evens look sparser, but still not one number is left out.
sets.infTask: Under the pairing n ↦ 3n, which number is the partner of 7?

logic.q1: What is the negation of “greater than 6”?
logic.q2: And, or, exclusive or: the mathematical “or” is not the one you think
logic.q4: If…, then…: when is it false, and what is its converse?
logic.q5: Do enough examples prove it? Euler’s prime formula
logic.q6: NIM: how do you always win?
logic.negIntro: “The number is greater than 6.” What is its negation? Not “less than 6”: 6 itself is left out of the original, so the negation has to contain it. Negation is the complement — it selects exactly the elements the original left out. Pick a property and switch the negation on and off.
logic.negDef1: Statement: a declarative sentence that is unambiguously either true or false; those two options are its truth value.
logic.negDef2: Negation: the negation of a statement P (¬P, read "not P") is the statement that is true exactly when P is false.
logic.negSentence2: ¬¬P: it is not true that the element is not {{p}}, that is, the element is {{p}}.
logic.negPairsTitle: Common negations, and the common mistake
logic.negPair_and_s: It is raining and the wind is blowing.
logic.negPair_and_w: It is not raining and the wind is not blowing.
logic.negPair_and_r: It is not raining or the wind is not blowing.
logic.negPair_all_r: There is a student who did not bring their book.
logic.negPair_some_s: There is a number that is negative.
logic.negPair_some_w: There is a number that is not negative.
logic.negTask: What is the negation of "The number is greater than 6."? Pick one, then compare the two selections: the negation must select exactly the elements the original left out.
logic.negHint: The negation of "greater than 6" must include 6 itself, since 6 is not greater than 6.
logic.negChoiceNotGt7: The number is not greater than 7.
logic.negChoiceLt7: The number is less than 7 but not 6.
logic.negTaskOriginal: The original statement is true for these elements:
logic.connIntro: “Tea or coffee?” — everyday “or” means one of the two. The mathematical “or” is inclusive: both being true is fine as well. Pick two properties, switch between the three connectives, and see which elements the compound statement is true for.
logic.connSentence_xor: The element is either {{a}} or {{b}} (but not both).
logic.vennConnAria: Venn diagram: the elements with properties A and B, the result of the connective shaded
logic.connRowHint: Each row of the table is one region of the diagram. Hover over a row!
logic.connOrNote: The mathematical “or” is inclusive: A ∨ B is true even when both are true. When everyday speech says “either…, or…”, that is the exclusive or: exactly one of the two.
logic.connTask: Select the elements that are either even or divisible by 3, in the exclusive sense!
logic.connHint: 6 and 12 are both even and divisible by 3. The exclusive or rules out exactly those.
logic.quantIntro: “Every element greater than 6 is even.” True? A single counterexample — 7, say — brings it down. “There is” works the other way round: one example confirms it. Build a statement and see what it turns into when you negate it.
logic.quantDef1: For all (∀): "every element …" is true when there is not a single exception. There is (∃): "there is an element that …" is true when at least one such element exists.
logic.quantDef2: Counterexample: a single case for which a "for all" statement fails. One counterexample brings the whole statement down.
logic.quantNoWitness: There is not a single example.
logic.quantNegSentence_all: Negation: There is an {{d}} that is not {{p}}. →
logic.quantNegNote: Notice that of the statement and its negation, exactly one is true. The negation of "every element is even" is not "no element is even" but "there is an element that is not even".
logic.quantTask: "Every element greater than 6 is even." This statement is false. Mark a counterexample!
logic.quantHint: A counterexample is an element that is greater than 6 but not even.
logic.impIntro: “If it rains, I take an umbrella.” That is a promise, and you can break it in only one way: it rains and you take no umbrella. If it does not rain, the promise holds whatever you do. Switch between the three modes and see which region can bring the statement down.
logic.impDef: Implication ("if P, then Q", P ⇒ Q): P is the premise, Q the conclusion. The statement is false only when P is true but Q is false; in every other case it is true.
logic.impConverseDef: Converse: the converse of “if P, then Q” is “if Q, then P”. It is a statement of its own, and its truth value may differ from the original’s.
logic.impSentence: If an element is {{p}}, then it is {{q}}. →
logic.impConverseSentence: Converse: If an element is {{q}}, then it is {{p}}. →
logic.iffSentence: An element is {{p}} if and only if it is {{q}}. →
logic.impCounter: Counterexample: {{list}}. For these the premise is true and the conclusion false.
logic.vennImpAria: Venn diagram: the elements with properties P and Q, the refuting regions shaded
logic.impRowHint: The shaded regions are where the statement can fail. Hover over a row!
logic.impContraNote: Contrapositive: “if not Q, then not P” always says the same as the original “if P, then Q” — try it with any setting. That is why a statement can be proved by proving its contrapositive. The converse, on the other hand, is not the same: it is a separate statement with its own truth value.
logic.impTask: Given the statement "If a number is divisible by 6, then it is even." Pick its converse, then decide whether the converse is true or false!
logic.impHint: In the converse, premise and conclusion swap without negation. Then look for an even number that is not divisible by 6.
logic.impChoice_converse: If a number is even, then it is divisible by 6.
logic.impChoice_inverse: If a number is not divisible by 6, then it is not even.
logic.impChoice_contrapositive: If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 6.
logic.proofIntro: Look at n² + n + 41: substituting n = 0, 1, 2, … gives prime after prime, and it keeps working for a good while. Step through the cases and find where it fails — and with it, whether many examples amount to a proof.
logic.proofDef: Theorem: a statement that has been proved. Proof: an argument that derives the statement from known truths by logical steps and covers all cases at once.
logic.proofStripAria: Values of n² + n + 41 for n from 0 to 44, primes in green, composite numbers in red
logic.proofNotPrime: n = {{n}}: {{value}} is not prime, because it is {{a}} · {{b}}.
logic.proofEulerMoral: The first {{first}} cases all give primes, and yet at n = {{first}} the claim fails. No number of examples is a proof, but a single counterexample is a refutation.
logic.proofTask: Theorem: the sum of two odd numbers is even. The steps below are the sentences of the proof, shuffled. Click them in the right order!
logic.proofHint: First name the things you are talking about; at the end, say why what you got is even.
logic.proofStep_name: Let the two odd numbers be 2k + 1 and 2m + 1, where k and m are integers.
logic.proofStep_conclude: k + m + 1 is an integer, so the sum is an integer multiple of 2, hence even.
logic.nimIntro: From a pile of matches you and the computer alternately take 1, 2 or 3, and whoever takes the last one wins. You start. Play a few rounds, then switch on the hint: one simple rule gives away every winning position.
logic.nimYouWin: You took the last one. You win!
logic.nimCpuWins: The computer took the last one. Turn on the hint and see where the game slipped away!
logic.nimHintLosing: The pile is a multiple of 4: there is no winning move from here unless the computer slips.
logic.nimHintTake_one: Winning move: take {{count}} so that {{left}} remain.
logic.nimHintTake_other: Winning move: take {{count}} so that {{left}} remain.
logic.nimStrategy: The strategy: if you leave your opponent a multiple of 4, whatever they take (1, 2 or 3) you can top it up to 4, and at the end the move 4 → 0 is yours. In other words: if the pile is not a multiple of 4, then the player to move can win. {{losing}}
logic.nimStartLosing: The current starting pile is a multiple of 4, so as the first player you can only win if the computer slips, and it will not. Pick another size!
logic.nimStartWinning: The current starting pile is not a multiple of 4, so as the first player you can win if you choose every move well.
logic.nimTask: There are 13 matches in the pile and it is your move. How many must you take so that good play from there on is sure to win?
logic.nimHint: You must leave your opponent a pile that is a multiple of 4. The largest such number below 13 is 12.

combi.q1: When do you multiply? The multiplication rule
combi.q2: When do you add, and when do you multiply?
combi.q3: How many orders, and what if two letters are the same?
combi.q4: Does the order matter? Team or podium
combi.q5: How many handshakes? Graphs and the complete graph
combi.q6: Can everyone know exactly three others?
combi.prodIntro: In the morning you pick one of 2 t-shirts and one of 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are there? Let us draw it. The first branching decides the t-shirt, the second the trousers, and the leaves of the tree are the finished outfits: 2 · 3 = 6.
combi.prodTreeAria: Choice tree with {{steps}} steps and {{total}} possibilities.
combi.prodTooMany: That is too many branches to draw: {{total}} possibilities. Remove a step or pick fewer options.
combi.prodLeaves: The number of leaves is the number of possibilities: {{total}}.
combi.prodRule: Multiplication rule: if a choice is made in several steps, and every step has the same number of options no matter what was chosen before, then the number of possibilities is the product of the options of the steps.
combi.prodTask: The canteen offers 3 soups, 4 main courses and 2 desserts. How many different lunches can you put together if you take exactly one of each?
combi.prodHint: Three steps one after the other, and none of them affects the others: multiply.
combi.sumIntro: The snack bar has 4 sandwiches and 3 pastries. If you buy one thing, you have 4 + 3 = 7 choices: the two cases never mix, so we add them up. But if you buy a sandwich and a pastry, the two decisions come one after the other: 4 · 3 = 12. Switch between the two views and watch what changes in the picture.
combi.sumAria_or: {{a}} dots in the first row and {{b}} dots in the second, {{total}} dots in total.
combi.sumAria_and: A grid of dots with {{b}} rows and {{a}} columns, {{total}} dots in total.
combi.sumRead_or: You pick a single thing from one of the two groups: {{a}} + {{b}} = {{total}} possibilities.
combi.sumRead_and: You pick one from each group, and every dot is one pair: {{a}} · {{b}} = {{total}} possibilities.
combi.sumRule: Addition rule: if you split the possibilities into cases that exclude each other, you add up the sizes of the cases. This is case separation: you cut a hard problem into a few easier ones.
combi.wrongProblem: Problem: how many two-digit numbers can be made from the digits 1, 2, 3 if the two digits must be different?
combi.wrongStep1: The first digit can be chosen in 3 ways.
combi.wrongStep2: The second digit can also be chosen in 3 ways.
combi.wrongTask: One step of this solution is wrong. Which one?
combi.wrongHint: Write out all the numbers: 12, 13, 21, 23, 31, 32. Then check how many options are really left for the second place.
combi.wrongFix: The second digit can only be chosen in 2 ways, because the first digit cannot be used again. Correctly, 3 · 2 = {{total}} two-digit numbers can be made.
combi.orderIntro: A few friends line up for a photo. In how many orders can they stand? We count systematically: with three friends the first place has 3 options, the second the remaining 2, the third only 1, that is 3 · 2 · 1 = 6. This is the multiplication rule again, with one option fewer at every step. Change the number of friends!
combi.orderTreeAria: Tree of orders for {{n}} friends, with {{total}} orders.
combi.orderTooMany: {{total}} branches are too many to draw. The table shows how fast this number grows.
combi.orderResult: {{n}} friends can line up in {{total}} different orders: that is exactly how many leaves the tree has.
combi.orderDef: n factorial (n!): the product of the integers from 1 to n, n! = n · (n − 1) · … · 2 · 1. It is the number of ways n different things can be arranged in order. By convention 0! = 1.
combi.orderRule: n things can be arranged in order in n! ways. The number grows frighteningly fast: ten people can already line up in more than three million ways.
combi.orderWordIntro: Let us rearrange the letters of the word {{word}}. If we could tell the two A's apart there would be {{all}} orders. But we cannot, so every word would appear on the list exactly twice: {{all}} has to be divided by 2.
combi.orderTask: Five friends sit down on a bench. {{first}} and {{second}} insist on sitting next to each other. How many seatings are possible?
combi.orderHint: Glue the two of them into a single block: then only 4 things have to be arranged. Inside the block the two of them can still swap places.
combi.selIntro: We pick three of five classmates. If they form a team, the order we list them in makes no difference: Anna–Bence–Csilla is the same team as Csilla–Anna–Bence. But if they stand on the podium — gold, silver, bronze — a different order means a different medal. Switch between the two views and see how much the number grows.
combi.selDef: Variation (in English books: k-permutation): choosing k out of n things where the order matters. Combination: choosing k out of n things where the order does not matter. Every combination corresponds to k! variations.
combi.selPickPrompt: Pick {{k}} people above and we will show you the orders they can stand in.
combi.selResult_no: The order does not matter, so {{total}} different teams can be put together.
combi.selResult_yes: Every team of {{k}} can stand on the podium in {{each}} different orders, so counting the medals there are {{teams}} · {{each}} = {{total}} cases.
combi.selNames: Instead of memorising the names, always ask the question: does the order matter? If yes, it is a variation; if not, a combination.
combi.selLottoTitle: How big is this number really?
combi.selLottoYears: Years at one ticket a week
combi.selLottoNote: That is how many ways 5 numbers can be chosen out of 90. Filling in a single ticket a week, this is how many years it would take to try them all.
combi.selTask: A team of 3 is put together from a club of 8 people. How many different teams are possible?
combi.selHint: There is no order inside a team. First work out the ordered count, 8 · 7 · 6, then divide it by 3! = 6.
combi.graphIntro: Draw the people as dots, and join two of them when they shook hands. That is all a graph is: it does not matter where the dots sit or whether the lines are straight — only what is joined to what. Click two vertices one after the other (or use the buttons) and see how many edges it takes for everyone to shake hands with everyone.
combi.graphDef: Graph: a set of dots, the vertices, and lines joining some of them, the edges. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges that run into it.
combi.graphResult: There are {{edges}} edges drawn now. If everyone shook hands with everyone, {{complete}} edges would be needed — exactly the number of ways to choose two of the {{n}} vertices.
combi.graphCompleteNote: If everyone shakes hands with everyone, every pair of vertices gets exactly one edge. So an edge is nothing but a choice of two vertices without order — exactly what we counted in the previous section.
combi.graphTask: There are 7 people at a party and everyone shakes hands with everyone else exactly once. How many handshakes are there?
combi.graphHint: Draw the complete graph on 7 vertices, or count like this: there are 7 · 6 handshake ends, but every handshake was counted twice.
combi.parityIntro: In a group everyone knows exactly three others. Is that possible with seven people? Add up the degrees: every acquaintance counts at two people, so the sum of the degrees can only be even. Set the head count and the degree, and see when such a graph can be drawn at all.
combi.parityPickD: How many others does everyone know?
combi.parityQuestion: Among {{n}} people everyone knows exactly {{d}} others. Is that possible?
combi.parityReason_ok: Yes, it is possible. The degrees would add up to {{sum}}, which means {{edges}} acquaintances, that is {{edges}} edges. One such graph is drawn below.
combi.parityReason_oddSum: Not possible. The degrees would add up to {{sum}}, which is odd — but the sum of the degrees is always twice the number of edges, so it is even.
combi.parityReason_degreeTooBig: Not possible. Nobody can know {{d}} others, because apart from themselves there are only {{n}} − 1 people.
combi.parityAria: Graph on {{n}} vertices where every vertex has degree {{d}}.
combi.parityNote: The sum of the degrees is always twice the number of edges, however you draw the graph. Every edge has two ends, and it adds one to the degree at each of them.
combi.parityTask: Can it happen that in a group of 9 people everyone knows exactly 3 others?
combi.parityHint: Multiply: 9 · 3 would be the sum of the degrees. But the sum of the degrees is always even.

num.towerTitle: 1. How the number sets are built on each other
num.towerIntro1: You learned to count with 1, 2, 3, … These are the natural numbers, and 0 belongs with them. But subtract 5 from 3 and you step out of them: you need −2 as well. Every new set of numbers is born this way — because some operation leads out of the old one.
num.towerIntro2: Click a number in the boxes. We show the narrowest set it belongs to. Watch out: the boxes are inside each other, so every natural number is an integer too, and every integer is rational too.
num.towerDef1: Natural numbers (ℕ): 0, 1, 2, 3, … — the counting numbers, with 0 included.
num.towerDef2: Integers (ℤ): the natural numbers and their opposites: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
num.towerDef3: Rational numbers (ℚ): the numbers that can be written as a quotient of two integers, in the form p/q with q ≠ 0. Their decimal form terminates or repeats.
num.towerDef4: Irrational numbers: the real numbers that cannot be written as a quotient of two integers. Their decimal form is endless and never repeats, for example √2 or π.
num.towerDef5: Real numbers (ℝ): the rational and the irrational numbers together. Every point of the number line is a real number, and every real number has its place on the line.
num.towerNone: Pick a number from the boxes and we will look at where it belongs.
num.towerSay_natural: This is a natural number: one of 0, 1, 2, 3, … So it is an integer and a rational number as well, since it can be written as a fraction, for example 7 = 7/1.
num.towerSay_integer: This is an integer but not a natural number, because it is negative. It is still rational, since it can be written as a fraction: −3 = −3/1.
num.towerSay_rational: This is a rational number: it can be written as one integer divided by another. It is not an integer, because on the number line it stands between two neighbouring whole numbers.
num.towerSay_irrational: This is an irrational number: no fraction p/q is equal to it. Its decimal form never stops and never falls into a repeating pattern.
num.towerWhyTitle: Why is a wider set always needed?
num.towerWhyZ: Subtraction leads out of the natural numbers. That is why the negative numbers are needed, and with them the integers, ℤ.
num.towerWhyQ: Division leads out of the integers. That is why fractions are needed, and with them the rationals, ℚ.
num.towerWhyR: Taking a root leads out of ℚ as well: no fraction squares to 2. That is why the real numbers, ℝ, are needed.
num.towerSetsLink: The ⊂ sign (subset) and the set operations are covered in detail in the Sets lesson.
num.towerTask: Which is the narrowest set of numbers the number belongs to? Choose in all five rows.
num.towerHint: Work out the roots first. If a number can be written as a fraction it is rational; if that fraction comes to a whole number it is an integer.
num.lawsTitle: 2. The laws of operations and the brackets
num.lawsIntro1: 3 · 4 or 4 · 3? The same thing. Turn a 3 × 4 rectangle and it becomes 4 × 3, but the number of little squares inside does not change. This is what being commutative means.
num.lawsIntro2: Drag the sliders and look at all three laws. Each says the same thing: the picture can be rearranged and the area stays. Addition and multiplication behave like this — subtraction and division do not.
num.lawsDef1: Commutativity: the order of the two terms does not matter. a + b = b + a and a · b = b · a.
num.lawsDef2: Associativity: the placing of the brackets does not matter. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) and (a · b) · c = a · (b · c).
num.lawsDef3: Distributivity: a sum can be multiplied term by term. a · (b + c) = a · b + a · c.
num.lawsAria_comm: Two rectangles: one {{a}} × {{b}} and one {{b}} × {{a}}, with the same number of little squares.
num.lawsAria_assoc: {{a}} + {{b}} + {{c}} little squares in a row, marked up with two different groupings.
num.lawsAria_distrib: A rectangle {{a}} units wide, cut into a part {{b}} units tall and a part {{c}} units tall.
num.lawsRead_comm: Both rectangles hold the same number of squares: in a product the order does not matter.
num.lawsRead_assoc: The same row of {{a}} + {{b}} + {{c}}, grouped in two ways. Where the brackets go makes no difference, the sum is the same.
num.lawsRead_distrib: The rectangle was cut across. The two pieces have areas {{a}} · {{b}} and {{a}} · {{c}}, and together they are the whole rectangle.
num.lawsNotComm: Subtraction and division are not commutative: swap the two numbers and the result changes. Here the order matters very much.
num.lawsParenNote: Without brackets, multiplication and division come first and only then addition and subtraction. A bracket overrides this: whatever is inside has to be worked out first.
num.lawsCalcNote: A calculator follows exactly the same order. If it says something else than you expected, you probably left out a bracket.
num.lawsTask: Work out 47 · 99 in your head using the distributive law.
num.fracIntro1: 1/4 and 0.25 are the same number, just written differently. You can switch from one to the other any time: a fraction really is a division, and the decimal form is the result of that division.
num.fracIntro2: Pick a numerator and a denominator and watch the steps of the division. The remainder is the interesting part: once an earlier remainder comes back, everything repeats from there on.
num.fracDef: Terminating decimal: the decimal digits run out, for example 1/4 = 0.25. Repeating decimal: a group of digits, the period, repeats for ever, for example 4/11 = 0.3636… The period is marked with a bar over it.
num.fracRemainderNote: A remainder can only be 0, 1, …, {{q}} − 1, so there are finitely many of them. Within {{q}} steps it therefore either hits 0 or repeats an earlier remainder. So every fraction has a decimal form that either stops or repeats.
num.fracStopRule: The decimal stops exactly when the denominator of the reduced fraction is built from 2s and 5s only. Those are the divisors of 10, and the decimal form works with powers of 10.
num.fracBackTitle: Back again: from a decimal to a fraction
num.fracBackIntro: If the decimal stops it is easy: 0.75 = 75/100. If it repeats you need a trick — multiply it by a power of ten and subtract it from itself.
num.fracBackNote: Multiplying by 10 only shifts the point. After two shifts the two numbers have the very same tail, so subtracting wipes the endless tail out and leaves a whole number.
num.fracTask: Write the number 0.363636… as a common fraction. Give the numerator and the denominator in lowest terms.
num.lineTitle: 4. The real numbers on the number line
num.lineIntro1: On the number line every real number has exactly one place, and every place holds exactly one number. Pick a number and we will show you where.
num.lineIntro2: A rational number’s decimal form either stops or repeats; an irrational one’s never settles. Their places are just as exact all the same: √2 is not “roughly” somewhere, it is at one definite point.
num.lineAria: Number line from −3 to 4, with {{name}} selected.
num.lineNoteRational: This is a rational number, so its decimal form stops or repeats: you can write it down exactly.
num.lineNoteIrrational: This is an irrational number. However many decimals you write down it is still only an approximation — but its place on the line is exact.
num.lineSqrtIntro: Stand a square of side 1 on the segment from 0 to 1. By Pythagoras its diagonal is √2 long. With a pair of compasses you can lay that length onto the number line.
num.lineSqrtAria: A unit square on the segment from 0 to 1, its diagonal swung onto the number line with an arc.
num.lineSqrtNote: No fraction writes this length down exactly, yet there it is on the line — a pair of compasses and a ruler find it. So irrational numbers are not something vague: they are points just as real as the rest.
num.lineZoomIntro: Pick a number and step further in. Each step cuts the interval into ten equal parts and asks which one the number falls into. The number of that part is exactly its next decimal digit.
num.lineZoomPickAria: Which number to zoom in on
num.lineZoomAria: The number line zoomed to {{level}} decimals, with {{name}} marked.
num.lineZoomNote_root2: The decimals of √2: {{digits}}… They never stop and never start repeating. That is the mark of an irrational number.
num.lineZoomNote_pi: The decimals of π: {{digits}}… Trillions of them have been worked out and nobody has found a pattern — nor will they, because π is irrational.
num.lineZoomNote_third: The decimals of 1/3: {{digits}}… The same 3 keeps coming. It is rational, and its period is a single digit long.
num.lineZoomNote_twentyTwoSevenths: The decimals of 22/7: {{digits}}… The block 142857 repeats for ever. This number is an old approximation of π, but it is not π: they part company at the third decimal.
num.lineTask: Which two neighbouring tenths does √10 fall between? Choose the lower one.
num.lineHint: Square them: 3.1² = 9.61, which is less than 10; 3.2² = 10.24, which is already more.
num.intervalIntro1: When we say "the numbers between 2 and 5", one question is always left open: do 2 and 5 themselves belong? Interval notation answers exactly that.
num.intervalIntro2: A filled circle: the endpoint is included, that end is closed. An empty circle: the endpoint is left out, that end is open. Switch the ends around and see what changes.
num.intervalDef1: Interval: one connected piece of the number line: the set of numbers lying between two endpoints.
num.intervalDef2: Closed interval [a, b]: both endpoints belong to it, that is a ≤ x ≤ b. Open interval (a, b): neither endpoint belongs, that is a < x < b. A half-open interval closes one end and opens the other.
num.intervalAria: An interval from {{from}} to {{to}}, its left end {{left}} and its right end {{right}}.
num.intWhyInside: It lies between the two endpoints.
num.intWhyLeftClosed: This is the left endpoint, and the left end is closed, so it is included.
num.intWhyLeftOpen: This is the left endpoint, but the left end is open, so it is left out.
num.intWhyRightClosed: This is the right endpoint, and the right end is closed, so it is included.
num.intWhyRightOpen: This is the right endpoint, but the right end is open, so it is left out.
num.intWhyBelow: It is smaller than the left endpoint.
num.intWhyAbove: It is bigger than the right endpoint.
num.intervalOtherNote: Hungarian textbooks turn the bracket outwards at an open end: what we write as (a, b) they write as ]a; b[. In a foreign textbook, always check which notation is in use.
num.intervalTask: Which interval is the set of the numbers x for which −1 < x ≤ 3?
num.intervalHint: Strictly greater than −1: −1 is left out, so the left end is open. Less than or equal to 3: 3 is included, so the right end is closed.
num.absIntro1: Three simple things you can do to a number: mirror it across 0, ask how far it is from 0, and find the partner that multiplies with it to give 1.
num.absDef1: Opposite (−x): the number that is as far from 0 as x, on the other side. The two add up to 0.
num.absDef2: Absolute value (|x|): the distance of the number from 0 on the number line. It is never negative.
num.absDef3: Reciprocal (1/x): the number that multiplied by x gives 1. Zero has no reciprocal.
num.absIntro2: Drag the slider and watch the three points. The opposite is always mirrored in 0. The farther a number is from 0, the closer its reciprocal sits to 0 — and 0 has no reciprocal at all.
num.absAria: Number line: x = {{x}}, its opposite {{opposite}}, and its reciprocal are all marked.
num.absFact1: A number and its opposite always add up to 0.
num.absFact2: A number times its reciprocal is always 1. That is why 0 has no reciprocal: multiplying by 0 never gives 1.
num.absFact3: An absolute value is never negative, and a number and its opposite have the same absolute value.
num.absFact4: The reciprocal of a fraction is that fraction turned upside down. So a number between 0 and 1 has a reciprocal bigger than 1.
num.absFact5: The absolute value of a difference is the distance of the two numbers on the line.
num.absTask: What is the opposite of the reciprocal of −3/4? Give the numerator and the denominator.
num.absHint: The reciprocal of −3/4 is that fraction turned over, so −4/3. Its opposite is the same number with the sign swapped.
num.estIntro1: Roughly how much is 398 · 51? Round both numbers to a single leading digit: 400 · 50 = 20 000. If the machine says 2 030, you mistyped something.
num.estIntro2: Estimating does not replace working it out, it comes before it. Once you know roughly how big the answer will be, a wrong keypress jumps out at you.
num.estDef1: Estimate: a quick approximation of the size of a result, done in your head with rounded numbers.
num.estDef2: Significant digit: the digits of a number starting from the first non-zero one. The first significant digit of 398 is 3; rounded to one significant digit it is 400.
num.estOff: The estimate is about {{percent}}% away from the exact value. That is plenty for checking how big the answer should be.
num.estRule: Estimate first, calculate second. If the machine says something else than you expected, check what you typed before you doubt the maths.
num.targetIntro: Use the digits {{digits}}, each of them exactly once, with the signs + − · : and brackets. Can you reach the target?
num.targetBadChars: Only digits, the signs + − · : and brackets may be used.
num.targetBadDigits: Each of the four digits ({{digits}}) has to be used exactly once.
num.targetBadExpr: I cannot work this one out. Check the brackets and the operation signs.
num.targetValue: The expression comes to {{value}}. Keep trying!
num.estTask: Five results somebody got with a calculator. Which are plausible and which are certainly wrong? Decide in your head, by estimating.
num.estHint: Round every number to one leading digit and work it out in your head. Watch the size: 612 : 3 is roughly 600 : 3 = 200.
num.roundIntro1: Rounding means throwing away the digits you do not need so that the number changes as little as possible. A single digit always decides whether it goes down or up.
num.roundIntro2: Pick a number and a place. The digits you keep stay in solid boxes, the deciding digit is highlighted and the dropped ones get a dashed box.
num.roundDef: Rounding: replacing a number by the nearest number that stops at a chosen place value. The first digit after the kept ones decides: 0 to 4 rounds down, 5 to 9 rounds up.
num.roundRule: 0–4 down, 5–9 up. The digits behind the deciding one no longer matter: even the ones after a 5 do not change the decision.
num.measureTitle: Measuring: how far can you trust the digits?
num.measureIntro: You measure the floor of the room: {{length}} m long and {{width}} m wide. Their product has plenty of decimals, but the tape was not that precise. Choose a measuring error.
num.measureDef: Measurement error: the possible gap between the measured value and the true value. If the tape is accurate to ±5 mm, the true length may differ from the reading by at most 5 mm in either direction.
num.measureSure: Only these digits are certain: {{sure}} m². The rest of {{nominal}} m² only looks precise — the measurement does not support it.
num.measureNote: A result can never be more precise than the measurement it came from. That is why rounding makes sense: the extra digits do not show knowledge, they hide what you do not know.
num.roundHint: The digit after the thousandths place is 5, so it rounds up.

pow.q8: The n-th root and fractional exponents
pow.defIntro1: 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 — that is long to write and easy to get wrong. Shorter: 2⁵. This shorthand is a power, and mathematics is full of them: areas, volumes, interest and data sizes are all written most simply with powers.
pow.defIntro2: Pick a base and drag the slider. Below it you can see how many factors are multiplied and what the result comes to.
pow.defDef1: Power: the notation aⁿ stands for the product of n factors, each equal to a. a is the base and n is the exponent. For example 2⁵ = 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 2 = 32: a product of five 2s.
pow.defDef2: First power: a¹ = a. The "product" of a single factor is the number itself, which is why the exponent 1 is usually not written out.
pow.defFactorsAria: {{factors}} identical factors side by side, each of them {{base}}.
pow.defSignNote: With a negative base the sign alternates: an even exponent gives a positive result, an odd one a negative result. Every further multiplication brings in one more minus, and two minuses cancel each other out.
pow.defTrapNote: (−2)⁴ and −2⁴ are not the same. With the bracket the minus belongs to the base, so it is a product of four negative numbers: positive. Without the bracket the exponent only applies to the 2 and the minus stays outside.
pow.defFoldTitle: How many times can you fold a sheet of paper?
pow.defFoldIntro: A sheet of paper is about 0.1 mm thick. Every fold doubles the number of layers — that is pure powering, 2ⁿ. Drag the slider and see how far the paper gets.
pow.defFoldStart: Nothing remarkable happens over the first few folds. Keep dragging.
pow.foldCmp7: 7 folds: 128 layers, about 1.3 cm. This is roughly where bare hands give up.
pow.foldCmp10: 10 folds: 1024 layers, about 10 cm — the length of a mobile phone.
pow.foldCmp14: 14 folds: more than 1.6 m — taller than you are.
pow.foldCmp20: 20 folds: about 105 m — longer than a football pitch.
pow.foldCmp23: 23 folds: about 840 m — taller than any building in the world.
pow.foldCmp30: 30 folds: about 107 km — the edge of space is usually drawn at 100 km.
pow.foldCmp42: 42 folds: about 440 000 km — past the Moon, which is 384 000 km away.
pow.defFoldRecord: In reality the paper runs out: nobody can fold a plain sheet more than eight times. The record is {{folds}} folds, set in {{year}}: Britney Gallivan managed it with a {{km}} km long strip of toilet paper.
pow.defHint: The bracket says the minus sign is part of the base. Without it the powering comes first, and only then does the minus go in front of the result.
pow.negIntro1: What is 2⁰? Multiplying something "zero times" means nothing, so the definition gives no answer. Instead we follow the pattern: walk down the exponents and watch what happens to the value.
pow.negIntro2: Each step lowers the exponent by one and divides the value by the base. Carry that step on below 0 and it settles by itself what 2⁰ and 2⁻¹ have to be.
pow.negDef1: Zeroth power: a⁰ = 1 for every a ≠ 0. This is not an arbitrary decision: dividing a¹ = a by a once more gives exactly 1, so it is the only value that keeps the pattern.
pow.negDef2: Negative exponent: a⁻ⁿ = 1 / aⁿ, where a ≠ 0. A negative exponent therefore means a reciprocal, not a negative number: 2⁻³ = 1/8, which is positive.
pow.negZeroNote: Find the row with exponent 0: the value there is 1. Below it come the negative exponents, and each step divides once more — which is how they turn into fractions.
pow.negTenNote: This is especially handy for powers of 10: 10⁻¹ = 0.1, 10⁻² = 0.01, 10⁻³ = 0.001. The negative exponent tells you which decimal place the 1 sits in. This is what normal form uses.
pow.negUndefNote: Two cases are left out. 0⁰ is not defined, and 0⁻¹ would be 1/0 — and we do not divide by zero.
pow.negTask: Write 5⁻² as a fraction. Give the numerator and the denominator.
pow.negHint: Work out 5 squared first, then turn the fraction upside down.
pow.lawsIntro1: 2³ · 2² = ? Do not multiply anything, just count. On the left there are three 2s, on the right two: five 2s together. So 2³ · 2² = 2⁵. Every law here comes from that one idea: count the factors.
pow.lawsIntro2: Pick a law, a base and the exponents. The little squares are the factors, and there are always exactly as many of them as the exponent says.
pow.lawsDef1: Product of powers with the same base: the base stays, the exponents are added.
pow.lawsDef2: Quotient of powers with the same base: the base stays, the exponents are subtracted. The base cannot be 0 here.
pow.lawsDef3: Power of a power: the base stays, the exponents are multiplied.
pow.lawsDef4: Power of a product: every factor of the product may be raised to the power on its own.
pow.lawsDef5: Power of a quotient: the numerator and the denominator may be raised to the power on their own. The denominator cannot be 0 here.
pow.lawsPictureAria: The factors arranged in groups, {{total}} little squares in total.
pow.lawsCancelNote: The same number stands above and below the fraction bar, so {{cancel}} pairs cancel. {{rest}} factors are left on top — exactly what the difference of the exponents says.
pow.lawsWhy: The picture is not an example, it is a proof. If the left side multiplies m copies of a by n copies of a, then m + n copies of a stand there — and that is precisely what aᵐ⁺ⁿ means. It holds for every positive whole m and n, not just for the values you set.
pow.lawsTrapTitle: What there is no law for
pow.lawsTrap: There is no rule for a sum. ({{a}} + {{b}})² comes to {{whole}}, while {{a}}² + {{b}}² is only {{parts}}. In the same way aᵐ + aⁿ cannot be merged into one power: the laws are about multiplying and dividing, not about adding.
pow.lawsTask: Write this as a single power: (3²)³ · 3⁴ : 3⁵. What is the exponent?
pow.lawsHint: Power of a power first: 2 · 3 = 6. Then the multiplication adds 4 and the division subtracts 5.
pow.sciIntro1: The Earth is 149 600 000 km from the Sun and a hydrogen atom is 0.0000000001 m across. Numbers like these are awkward to write down and even more awkward to compare: you end up counting zeros one by one.
pow.sciIntro2: Astronomers and biologists therefore write them differently. Move the point until a single digit is left in front of it, and note how many places you moved it. Try it with the slider.
pow.sciDef: Normal form: a number written as a · 10ᵏ, where a falls between 1 and 10 (1 ≤ a < 10) and k is a whole number. a does not have to be whole: it is usually a decimal such as 1.496 or 5.2, with exactly one non-zero digit before the point. a carries the significant digits of the number and k carries its size.
pow.sciPreset_earthSun: Distance from the Earth to the Sun
pow.sciPreset_redCell: The diameter of a red blood cell
pow.sciPreset_hydrogen: The diameter of a hydrogen atom
pow.sciDigitsAria: The digits of the number, with the decimal point after digit {{before}}.
pow.sciPickShift: How many places do we move the point?
pow.sciNote1: The exponent says how many places the point moved. It is positive for large numbers and negative for numbers below 1. Instead of counting zeros you only have to remember one number.
pow.sciNote2: On a calculator display this looks like 1.496E8, or sometimes 1.496 08. It is the same thing, with the "· 10" left out.
pow.sciHint: Move the point four places to the right, so that it lands in front of the 5. That is why the exponent is negative.
pow.sciCalcIntro1: How many seconds does a person live? A year has about 3.15 · 10⁷ seconds. Counting eighty years, 80 · 3.15 · 10⁷ ≈ 2.52 · 10⁹ — roughly two and a half billion seconds.
pow.sciCalcIntro2: In normal form a multiplication falls apart into two easy steps: multiply the first factors, add the exponents of 10. Move the sliders and watch both steps.
pow.sciCalcDef1: Multiplying in normal form: the first factors are multiplied and the exponents of 10 are added.
pow.sciCalcDef2: Dividing in normal form: the first factors are divided and the exponents of 10 are subtracted. If the first factor of the result leaves the range between 1 and 10, the point is moved one more step back.
pow.sciCalcSameNote: This step is not needed now: the first factor is already between 1 and 10.
pow.sciCalcFactIntro: The internet is full of very large and very small numbers. The order of magnitude — the exponent of 10 — gives away in a moment when somebody has miscounted. Decide for each claim whether it is believable.
pow.sciClaim_hair: The thickness of a human hair
pow.sciClaim_yearSec: The length of a year in seconds
pow.sciClaim_cells: The number of cells in a human body
pow.sciCalcTask: Six claims, each with a number in normal form. Which are believable and which are out by orders of magnitude? Decide on all six.
pow.sciCalcHint: Convert to a unit you know. 10⁻⁵ m is a hundredth of a millimetre, and 10¹² is a thousand billion — there are certainly not that many people on Earth.
pow.sqrtIntro1: A square plot has an area of 49 m². How long is its side? 7 m, because 7 · 7 = 49. And if the area is 50 m²? Then the side falls between 7 and 8. Asking the question backwards like this is taking a root: the square is given, the side is wanted.
pow.sqrtIntro2: Drag the slider and watch the side of the square grow with the area. The length of the side is exactly the square root of the area.
pow.sqrtDef: Square root: the square root of a number a ≥ 0 is the non-negative number whose square is a. It is written √a. For example √49 = 7, because 7 ≥ 0 and 7² = 49.
pow.sqrtAria: A square of area {{area}} units, with a side of {{side}} units.
pow.sqrtExactNote: {{area}} is a perfect square, so its root is a whole number: √{{area}} = {{root}}. The side of the square can be labelled exactly.
pow.sqrtBetweenNote: √{{area}} is not a whole number: it falls between {{lo}} and {{hi}}, because {{loSq}} < {{area}} < {{hiSq}}. Always run this check before believing what the machine printed.
pow.sqrtTableTitle: Perfect squares worth knowing by heart
pow.sqrtCalcIntro: Type in a non-negative number. We show its root to four decimals and, next to it, which two whole numbers it has to fall between. A mistyped digit shows up at once.
pow.sqrtCalcNote: The root key of a calculator gives a rounded value. √2 ≈ 1.4142, but 1.4142² = 1.99996…, not exactly 2. The exact value has infinitely many decimals: √2 is an irrational number.
pow.sqrtTrap1: √(−4) does not exist among the real numbers: no real number has a negative square. That is why we required a ≥ 0.
pow.sqrtTrap2: √(x²) is |x|, not x. For example √((−3)²) = √9 = 3, not −3. A root is never negative, even when a negative number was squared.
pow.sqrtHint: The square first: (−7)² = 49. Then the root, which is never negative.
pow.sqrtLawsIntro1: √(4 · 9) = √36 = 6, and √4 · √9 = 2 · 3 = 6. The same answer, and that is no coincidence: a product or a quotient under the root sign can be split apart.
pow.sqrtLawsIntro2: Pick two numbers and compare the two sides. Whatever you choose, both routes give the same value.
pow.sqrtLawsDef1: Root of a product: √(a · b) = √a · √b, when a ≥ 0 and b ≥ 0.
pow.sqrtLawsDef2: Root of a quotient: √(a / b) = √a / √b, when a ≥ 0 and b > 0.
pow.sqrtLawsTrapTitle: There is no rule for a sum here either
pow.sqrtLawsTrap: √({{a}} + {{b}}) comes to {{whole}}, but √{{a}} + √{{b}} is already {{parts}}. A root cannot be split across a sum — this is the most common mistake in the whole topic.
pow.sqrtLawsSimpTitle: Taking a factor out of the root
pow.sqrtLawsSimpIntro: If there is a perfect-square factor under the root, it can be moved out in front of the root sign. That gives a shorter and exact form, with no rounding.
pow.sqrtLawsSimpNote: The largest perfect square that divides {{n}} is {{square}}, so its root, {{root}}, is what comes out in front.
pow.sqrtLawsTask: Write √48 in the form a·√b, with b as small as possible.
pow.sqrtLawsHint: Look for the largest perfect square that divides 48. It is 16, and 48 = 16 · 3.
pow.nthTitle: 8. The n-th root and fractional exponents
pow.nthIntro1: A cube has a volume of 27 cm³. How long is its edge? 3 cm, because 3³ = 27. This is the cube root: the same idea as the square root, one power higher. Ask with a fifth power and you are looking for a fifth root.
pow.nthIntro2: Pick the root index and the number. When the result is a whole number we say so.
pow.nthDef1: n-th root: the n-th root of a number a is the number whose n-th power is a. It is written ⁿ√a. For even n we need a ≥ 0 and take the non-negative root; for odd n any a works, for example ∛(−8) = −2.
pow.nthOddNote: With an odd root index a negative number is fine too: ∛(−8) = −2, because (−2)³ = −8. With an even index there is no real answer, just as there is none for √(−4).
pow.nthFracIntro: What if the exponent were not a whole number but a fraction? Nothing stops us from inventing a meaning — but only one meaning keeps the laws of section 3 true.
pow.nthDef2: Fractional (rational) exponent: the exponent 1/n means taking the n-th root, and the exponent m/n means a root and a power together — it does not matter which you do first. The base here is a positive number.
pow.nthWhy: Apply the "power of a power" rule to the exponent 1/2. The exponents multiply, so the result is the base itself. In other words, the power with exponent 1/2 is the number whose square is the base — and that is exactly what the square root means. No other choice is left.
pow.nthTask: Work this out: 16 to the power 3/4.
pow.nthHint: The fourth root first: the fourth root of 16 is 2. Then cube it: 2³ = 8.

alg.q1: Think of a number, and I will guess it
alg.q5: The named identities: (a + b)² and (a − b)²
alg.q6: The difference of two squares: (a + b)(a − b)

alg.trickTitle: 1. Think of a number, and I will guess it
alg.trickIntro1: Think of a number. Add 5. Multiply it by 2. Subtract 10. Divide by 2. I can guess it: you got back exactly the number you thought of. This is not magic and it is not guesswork — the trick works for every number, and you are about to see why.
alg.trickIntro2: The secret is to write a letter where the number you thought of would go. x can be any number, so if the steps end on x, the trick works for every number. Pick a trick, set what you thought of, and follow the two columns.
alg.trickDef1: Algebraic expression (an expression with letters): an expression built from numbers, letters and operation signs, for example 2x + 10 or 3a − b. The letter stands in for a number we do not know, or one that could be anything.
alg.trickDef2: Variable: the letter in the expression. x is not a secret particular number; it is a place any number can be written into.
alg.trickDef3: Value of an expression: the number the expression gives once a particular number is written in place of the letter. The value of 2x + 10 at x = 4 is 2 · 4 + 10 = 18.
alg.trickStep_addNext: Add the number one bigger than this one
alg.trickStep_subSecret: Subtract the number you thought of
alg.trickEndsX: The last row is x, so the number you thought of always comes back. That is why the trick works for any number at all.
alg.trickEndsConst: There is no x in the last row, only {{value}}. The result therefore does not depend on the number you thought of: everyone gets the same one.
alg.trickTask: Here is a new trick: think of a number, multiply it by 4, add 8, divide by 4, and finally subtract the number you thought of. What always comes out?
alg.trickHint: Write it with x: 4x, then 4x + 8, then x + 2, and subtract the x at the end.
alg.termsIntro1: The expression 3x² + 5x − 2x² + 7 − x + 4 is long, even though the same thing can be said more briefly. For that you need to know what belongs together in it. The pluses and minuses cut the expression into terms, and only terms of the same kind can be added: the x² ones with the x² ones, the x ones with the x ones, the plain numbers with each other.
alg.termsDef1: Sum and term: an expression joined by addition (or subtraction) is a sum, and its parts are the terms. 3x² + 5x − 7 has three terms: 3x², 5x and −7. The minus sign belongs to its term.
alg.termsDef2: Product and factor: an expression joined by multiplication is a product, and its parts are the factors. The factors of 3x² are 3, x and x.
alg.termsDef3: Coefficient: the number at the front of a term. The coefficient of 3x² is 3, the coefficient of −x is −1, and the coefficient of 7 is 7 itself.
alg.termsDef4: Like terms: terms whose letter part is the same, so that only the coefficient may differ. 3x² and −2x² are like terms; 3x² and 5x are not. Only like terms can be collected together.
alg.termsDef5: Polynomial: an expression built from numbers and letters using only addition, subtraction and multiplication, so no letter sits in a denominator or under a root. x² + 4x + 11 is a polynomial; 1/x is not.
alg.termsNote: 3x² + 5x is neither 8x⁵ nor 8x³: two different kinds of term cannot be written as one. But 3x² · 5x is 15x³ — that is multiplication, and the next section is about it.
alg.termsTask: Collect: 4a + 7b − a + 2b − 3. Give the coefficient of a, of b, and the number.
alg.termsHint: Only like terms add up. The −3 has no partner, so it stays as it was.
alg.opsIntro1: Let us start with the simple case: one term multiplied by one term. 2x²y · 3xy³ looks frightening, but once you write out the factors only tidying is left: the numbers next to each other, the x's next to each other, the y's next to each other. That is why the exponents add up — the same rule as in the Powers, roots lesson.
alg.opsDef: Monomial: an algebraic expression with no addition or subtraction in it, only a product of numbers and letters, for example 2x²y, −5a or 7. 2x + 1 already has two terms.
alg.opsAria_mul: The factors of the two monomials side by side, and below them the same factors regrouped: numbers first, then the x's, then the y's.
alg.opsAria_pow: The factors of the base repeated as many times as the exponent says, and below them the same factors regrouped.
alg.opsAria_div: The factors of the product and the factors of the divisor, and below them the factors that are left.
alg.opsRegroup_div: What is left after the division:
alg.opsDivNote: Division is multiplication read backwards. Divide a product by one of its factors and the other factor is what remains: the numbers are divided and the exponents are subtracted.
alg.opsNote1: Do not mix addition up with multiplication: 2x² + 3x² = 5x², because that makes five x² terms, but 2x² · 3x² = 6x⁴, because there the numbers multiply and the exponents add.
alg.opsNote2: When a product is raised to a power, every factor is raised, not just the letter: (2x²)³ = 2³ · (x²)³ = 8x⁶.
alg.opsTask: (3a²b)² = ? Give the coefficient and the two exponents.
alg.opsHint: Write it out: (3a²b)² = 3a²b · 3a²b. The numbers multiply, and the exponents of the same letter add.
alg.expandIntro1: 3 · (x + 4) is three copies of (x + 4) side by side: 3x + 12. In the picture that is a rectangle with one side 3 and the other x + 4. You can work out its area in two ways: in one piece, or by adding the two parts separately. The two results agree — that is expanding a bracket.
alg.expandIntro2: If both factors have two terms, the rectangle falls into four parts. The pieces of (x + 3)(x + 2) are x², 3x, 2x and 6, which collect to x² + 5x + 6. Move the sliders and watch how the middle term is always the sum of the two numbers and the last one their product.
alg.expandDef1: Identity: an equality that holds for every value of the letters. 3(x + 4) = 3x + 12 is an identity: whatever you write in place of x, the two sides are equal.
alg.expandDef2: Factoring: writing a sum as a product. It is expanding read backwards: 3x + 12 = 3(x + 4).
alg.expandDef3: Factoring out: the simplest way to factor. If the same factor appears in every term, we take it out in front of the bracket: 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3), 4x² + 6x = 2x(2x + 3).
alg.expandRule: Expanding a bracket: a(b + c) = ab + ac. Every term inside the bracket has to be multiplied by the factor in front of it, not just the first one.
alg.expandPickK: The number in front of the bracket
alg.expandAria_one: A rectangle with one side {{k}} and the other x + {{a}}. It is split in two: one part is the x part, the other is the number.
alg.expandAria_two: A rectangle split into four parts: the big x² square, an x rectangle beside it and another below it with sides {{a}} and {{b}}, and the product of the two numbers in the corner.
alg.expandSumProduct: The middle term is {{a}} + {{b}} = {{sum}}, and the last one is {{a}} · {{b}} = {{product}}.
alg.expandTask: Expand: (x + 4)(x + 5) = x² + □x + □. What goes in the two boxes?
alg.expandHint: The middle coefficient is the sum of 4 and 5, and the last number is their product.
alg.squareTitle: 5. The named identities: (a + b)² and (a − b)²
alg.squareIntro1: What is 31²? You can do it in your head: 31 = 30 + 1, and the square (30 + 1)² falls into four pieces: 30², twice 30 · 1, and 1². That is 900 + 60 + 1 = 961. This is not a trick that only works for 31; it is true of the square of every sum — which is how it earned its name.
alg.squareIntro2: You can see the square (a + b)² in the picture: its side is a + b, and inside it, next to an a² square and a b² square, sit two identical rectangles of area a · b. That is where the 2ab in the middle comes from, and that is why (a + b)² is not equal to a² + b².
alg.squareIntro3: If the bracket has a subtraction in it, almost the same thing happens: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b². In the picture we cut a strip of width b twice off a square of side a, but the corner was cut away twice, so the b² has to be given back once.
alg.squareDef1: Named identity: an identity used so often that it is worth knowing by heart. The three most important ones are (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² and (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
alg.squareDef2: Perfect square: an expression that can be written as the square of a two-term expression. x² + 6x + 9 is a perfect square, because it is (x + 3)²; x² + 6x + 10 is not.
alg.squareAriaPlus: A square of side {{a}} + {{b}} split into four parts: an a² square, two identical a · b rectangles and a b² square.
alg.squareAriaMinus: A square of side {{a}} with the (a − b)² square in its top left corner, a strip of width {{b}} beside it and another below it, and the b² square in the bottom right corner.
alg.squareReadPlus: The big square has side {{a}} + {{b}}, and its area is the sum of the four parts. The two identical rectangles are what make the 2ab: that is why (a + b)² = a² + b² is not true.
alg.squareReadMinus: The big square is the a², and the little square of side {{rest}} in the top left corner is the (a − b)² we are after. The two strips of width {{b}} come to 2ab together, but where they overlap the b² was taken away twice, so it has to be given back once.
alg.squareMentalTitle: In your head: squaring two-digit numbers
alg.squareMentalNote: We always work from the nearest round ten, so the small part is at most 5 and its square at most 25 — little enough to keep in your head.
alg.squareTask: Work it out in your head: 52² = ?
alg.diffTitle: 6. The difference of two squares: (a + b)(a − b)
alg.diffIntro1: What is 99 · 101? Write it like this: (100 − 1)(100 + 1). Expand the brackets and the −100 and the +100 cancel each other, leaving 100² − 1² = 9999. This is the third named identity: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
alg.diffIntro2: In the picture we cut a corner of side b out of a square of side a. The L shape that is left can be rearranged into a single rectangle with sides a + b and a − b. The same area in two shapes — which is why the identity holds. Press the Rearrange button.
alg.diffIntro3: This identity also helps with questions of divisibility. The number one less than the square of an odd number is always divisible by 8: n² − 1 = (n − 1)(n + 1), and for odd n the two neighbours are consecutive even numbers, one of which is divisible by 4 as well.
alg.diffRule: The third named identity: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². When the brackets are expanded, the two mixed terms, −ab and +ab, cancel each other, which is why only the difference of the two squares is left.
alg.diffAriaBefore: A square of side {{a}} with a square of side {{b}} missing from its bottom right corner. The remaining L shape is split into two rectangles.
alg.diffAriaAfter: The same two rectangles laid end to end: one rectangle {{a}} + {{b}} wide and {{a}} − {{b}} high.
alg.diffRead: The rearranged rectangle is {{width}} units wide and {{height}} units high, so its area is {{value}} — exactly the difference of the two squares.
alg.diffPickD: How far we step from it
alg.diffTask: Work it out in your head: 39 · 41 = ?
alg.diffHint: 39 = 40 − 1 and 41 = 40 + 1, so 40² − 1² is what is left.
alg.solveIntro1: Solving an equation uses the same rewrites as everything so far: expanding brackets, collecting like terms, spotting a named identity. A good rewrite does not change the solution; it only puts the equation into a simpler shape. Pick an equation and step through the solution.
alg.solveIntro2: Factoring is so useful in equations because a product can only be zero if one of its factors is zero. That turns x² − 25 = 0 into two easy equations: x − 5 = 0 or x + 5 = 0.
alg.solveDef: Root of an equation (its solution): the number which, written in place of the letter, makes the two sides of the equation equal. The root of 2x + 1 = 7 is 3, because 2 · 3 + 1 = 7. An equation can have more than one root: both 5 and −5 are roots of x² = 25.
alg.solveZeroRule: A product is zero if and only if at least one of its factors is zero. That is why (x − 5)(x + 5) = 0 holds exactly when x − 5 = 0 or x + 5 = 0.
alg.stepSubBoth: We subtract the same thing from both sides.
alg.stepDivBoth: We divide both sides by the same number.
alg.stepCancelSq: The x² is the same on both sides, so it drops out.
alg.stepFactorDiff: A difference of two squares: we factor it.
alg.stepFactorSquare: A perfect square: we write it as (x + 3)².
alg.stepZeroProduct: A product is only zero if one of its factors is zero.
alg.stepZeroSquare: A square is only zero if what is being squared is zero.
alg.solveTask: Which named identity is hiding in each of them? Choose one for all six expressions.
alg.solveHint: Look at the middle term: in a perfect square it is twice the product of the two square roots. If there is no middle term and a minus sits between the two squares, it is a difference of two squares.
alg.completeTitle: 8. Completing the square and the parabola
alg.completeIntro1: x² + 6x + 5 is not a perfect square, but it is nearly one: x² + 6x + 9 would be, because it is (x + 3)². So let us add the 9 and take it straight back off again, so that nothing changes: x² + 6x + 5 = (x² + 6x + 9) − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4. The picture shows what is missing: the x² and the two 3x strips form a square whose corner is exactly the empty bit.
alg.completeIntro2: Why is this useful? (x + 3)² is never negative, its smallest value is 0, and that happens at x = −3. So the smallest value of x² + 6x + 5 is −4, taken exactly at x = −3. The new shape hands you the lowest point of the graph — the single most important thing to know when drawing it. Move the sliders and watch the parabola move.
alg.completeDef: Completing the square: putting an expression of the form x² + px + q into the form (x + h)² + k. Here h is half of p, and k is the correction the added h² calls for: k = q − h².
alg.completeAria: A square of side x with a strip of width {{h}} beside it and another below it, and in the corner, drawn with a dashed line, the missing little square of area {{square}}.
alg.completeNoPicture: The picture shows the case of a positive p.
alg.completeVertex: The lowest point: at x = {{x}} the value is {{k}}.
alg.completeTask: Complete the square: x² − 8x + 3 = (x + □)² + □. Write in the two numbers, with their signs.
alg.completeHint: Half of −8 is −4, and the (−4)² = 16 has to be taken away again.

prop.directIntro1: A kilo of apples costs 600 Ft. Two kilos cost 1200 Ft, half a kilo 300 Ft, ten kilos 6000 Ft. However you change the quantity, the price changes with it in the same way: twice as many apples cost twice as much. This is direct proportion, and everyday life is full of it: the price of petrol, an hourly wage, the data you download.
prop.directIntro2: This is easy to check in a table. Divide the price by the quantity: if the same number comes out in every row, it is a direct proportion. That number is the unit price, and in the formula it is the constant of proportionality.
prop.directDef1: Direct proportion: two quantities are directly proportional if whenever one grows by some factor, the other grows by the same factor. Their quotient is then constant: y / x = k, that is, y = k · x.
prop.directDef2: Constant of proportionality: the number k you multiply one quantity by to get the other. In the apple example k = 600 Ft/kg.
prop.directConstant: The last column holds the same number in every row: {{k}}. That is the unit price, the constant of proportionality.
prop.directDoubled: {{x}} → {{x2}}: twice the quantity, {{y}} → {{y2}}: twice the value.
prop.directNote: The graph is a straight line through the origin: zero quantity costs zero, and every step raises it by the same amount.
prop.directTask: Which table shows a direct proportion?
prop.directHint: Divide y by x in every row. Only one of the tables gives the same number each time.
prop.inverseIntro1: You are sharing a pizza of 24 slices. If there are two of you, everyone gets 12 slices, if six, 4, if twelve, 2. The more of you there are, the less each one gets — but not in an arbitrary way: twice as many people get half as much each. This is inverse proportion.
prop.inverseIntro2: Here it is not the quotient but the product that stays constant: the number of people times the slices each always makes 24. The same happens with speed and travel time, or with the number of workers and the time a job takes.
prop.inverseDef: Inverse proportion: two quantities are inversely proportional if whenever one grows by some factor, the other shrinks to the same fraction of itself. Their product is then constant: x · y = k, that is, y = k / x.
prop.inverseLblX_pizza: How many of you there are
prop.inverseConstant: Their product is the same wherever you put the slider: {{x}} · {{y}} = {{k}}.
prop.inverseDoubled: {{x}} → {{x2}}: twice as many, {{y}} → {{y2}}: half as much.
prop.inverseNote: The graph is a curve that flattens out but never reaches the axes: however many of you there are, everyone gets something, and however little each gets, there is some number of you.
prop.inverseTask: Six workers paint a school in 10 days. How many days does the same job take four workers?
prop.inverseHint: First work out the whole job in worker-days: 6 · 10. Then divide that by 4.
prop.graphsTitle: 3. Graphs of proportions — and what is not one
prop.graphsIntro1: Many quantities change together without being proportional. A taxi fare grows with the distance, but there is a fixed charge, so even zero kilometres are not free — the graph is a straight line, only it does not start at the origin. A person’s height grows with their age, but no formula ties the two together. We speak of proportion only when the connection is exact: a quotient, a product, or something else that stays constant.
prop.graphsIntro2: Besides direct and inverse proportion there are other regular connections. The area of a square is proportional to the square of its side: twice the side is four times the area. The other way round, the side is proportional to the square root of the area. Pick a situation and see which curve belongs to it.
prop.graphsDef1: Quadratic proportion: one quantity is proportional to the square of the other: y = k · x². If x doubles, y grows fourfold.
prop.graphsDef2: Square-root proportion: one quantity is proportional to the square root of the other: y = k · √x. If x grows fourfold, y only doubles.
prop.graphKind_linear: a line, but not a proportion: y = k · x + b
prop.graphAria_direct: A straight line rising steadily from the origin.
prop.graphAria_inverse: A falling curve that flattens out but never reaches the axes.
prop.graphAria_linear: A straight line rising steadily, starting above the origin rather than at it.
prop.graphAria_square: A curve rising ever more steeply: the right half of a parabola.
prop.graphAria_root: A rising curve that flattens out but never turns back.
prop.graphsPickPrompt: Pick a situation and the curve that belongs to it lights up.

prop.sit_taxi: a taxi fare against the distance
prop.sit_squareArea: the area of a square against its side
prop.sit_areaSide: the side of a square against its area

prop.sitWhy_apples: Twice as many apples cost twice as much, and 0 kg costs 0 Ft: direct proportion.
prop.sitWhy_taxi: There is a fixed charge, so 0 km is not 0 Ft: a line, but not through the origin.
prop.sitWhy_speedTime: Twice the speed means half the time: their product, the distance, stays constant.
prop.sitWhy_squareArea: Twice the side gives four times the area: quadratic.
prop.sitWhy_areaSide: Four times the area gives twice the side: a square-root connection.
prop.sitWhy_ageHeight: They grow together, but no formula ties them: none of the curves.
prop.graphsTask: What connects the two quantities? Decide it for all eight.
prop.graphsHint: Ask yourself: if one quantity doubles, what happens to the other? It doubles, it halves, it grows fourfold — or none of these.
prop.unitsIntro1: Converting units is a direct proportion too: 1 km is 1000 m, so 2.5 km is 2500 m — we always multiply by a thousand. For lengths each rung of the ladder is a factor of ten. For areas it is a hundred, because a square of side 1 m holds 10 · 10 = 100 squares of side 1 dm. For volumes it is a thousand: 10 · 10 · 10.
prop.unitsIntro2: For time the rungs are not tens: 60 seconds make a minute, 60 minutes an hour, 24 hours a day. For speed two units change at once: 1 m/s means one metre every second, so 3600 metres, that is 3.6 km, every hour. This is why 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.
prop.unitsDef: Derived unit: a unit built from several base units, for example m/s (metres per second), km/h or Ft/kWh. When converting, every unit inside it has to be converted.
prop.unitsLadderAria: The ladder of units from the smallest to the largest, with the factor written between neighbouring rungs.
prop.unitsStepsDown: We change to a smaller unit, so we multiply. The whole factor: {{factor}}.
prop.unitsStepsUp: We change to a larger unit, so we divide. The whole divisor: {{factor}}.
prop.unitsStepsSame: The two units are the same, there is nothing to convert.
prop.unitsNote: 1 ml = 1 cm³, 1 l = 1 dm³, 1 m³ = 1000 l — the units of liquids and the units of volume measure the same thing.
prop.unitsInvalid: That is not a number. Type a decimal, for example 2.5.
prop.unitsHint: 72 km is 72 000 m and one hour is 3600 seconds. Divide one by the other.
prop.percentTitle: 5. The base, the value and the rate of a percentage
prop.percentIntro1: A coat of 15 000 Ft is on sale at 20% off. A percentage is a proportion too: 1% is a hundredth of the whole and 20% is twenty times that. The whole we compute from is the 15 000 Ft; the size of the discount is the 20%; the amount taken off is the 3000 Ft. These three numbers always travel together, and any two of them give the third.
prop.percentIntro2: There are three kinds of question: how much is 20% of it (we are looking for the value), what percentage is it (we are looking for the rate), and 3000 is 20% of what (we are looking for the base). Pick the one that is missing and watch the formula.
prop.percentDef2: Base: the whole the percentage is taken of. In the coat example it is 15 000 Ft.
prop.percentDef3: Rate: the size of the percentage, the number in front of the percent sign. In the example it is 20.
prop.percentDef4: Percentage value: the given percentage of the base, the amount we end up with. In the example it is 3000 Ft.
prop.unknown_value: I am looking for the value
prop.unknown_rate: I am looking for the rate
prop.unknown_base: I am looking for the base
prop.percentBarAria: A horizontal bar: its whole length is the base, its shaded part is the percentage value.
prop.percentTask: A pair of shoes of 24 000 Ft is sold for 18 000 Ft. What percentage is the discount?
prop.percentHint: The discount in forints is 6000. The base is the original price, 24 000.
prop.changeTitle: 6. Percentage change and the percentage point
prop.changeIntro1: The price of something goes up by 20% and then down by 20%. Do we get the original price back? No: the 20% drop is computed from the raised price, so it takes off more than the rise added. We end up at 96% of the original price.
prop.changeIntro2: The simplest way to compute it: a 20% rise is multiplying by 1.2, a 20% drop is multiplying by 0.8. Two changes one after the other are two multiplications: 1.2 · 0.8 = 0.96. Set the two steps and watch the multipliers.
prop.changeIntro3: When the percentage itself changes, one has to be careful with words. If a bank pays 4% interest instead of 3%, that is a rise of one percentage point — but the interest grew by 33%, because 4 is 133% of 3. The news often mixes the two up.
prop.changeDef: Percentage point: the difference of two percentages. From 3% to 4% the change is one percentage point, even though that is a third more interest.
prop.changeRule: The multiplier: a rise of p% is multiplying by (1 + p/100), a drop of p% is multiplying by (1 − p/100). This is how several changes melt into a single product.
prop.changePercent: The change in percent: {{pct}}%. The new rate is {{ratio}}% of the old one.
prop.changeTask: The price of something rose by 25% and then fell by 20%. What percentage of the original price is it now?
prop.changeAnswerLabel: As a percentage of the original price
prop.billIntro1: An electricity bill is not a single number. It has the consumption in kilowatt-hours, the unit price (how many forints one kilowatt-hour costs), the energy charge computed from these, a fixed fee that is due even if you use nothing, and the VAT at the end. Drag the consumption and watch how each line changes.
prop.billIntro2: Notice that the energy charge is directly proportional to the consumption, but the amount payable is not, because the fixed fee does not depend on it. If you use twice as much, the bill will not be twice as big. This is why it is worth looking at the unit price and the fixed fee separately when you compare providers.
prop.billDef1: Unit price: the price of one unit of something, for example Ft/kWh, Ft/m³ or Ft/kg. The unit price is the constant of proportionality between the quantity and the charge.
prop.billDef2: Net and gross price: the net price is the price without VAT, the gross is what is payable with VAT included. At 27% VAT, gross = net · 1.27.
prop.billCompare: Show it at twice the consumption
prop.billCompareNote: Twice the consumption: the energy charge doubles, but the amount payable is only {{ratio}} times as much.
prop.billShare: The energy charge is {{share}}% of the amount payable; the rest is the fixed fee and the VAT.
prop.billTask: A consumption of 150 kWh, a unit price of 36 Ft/kWh, a fixed fee of 1200 Ft and 27% VAT. How much is payable?
prop.billHint: The energy charge first: 150 · 36. Add the fixed fee, then multiply by 1.27.
prop.interestIntro1: If you put 100 000 Ft in the bank at 5% a year, after one year you have 105 000 Ft. In the second year you get 5% of that, so not 5000 but 5250 Ft. The money grows by the same multiplier year after year: 1.05 · 1.05 · … — this is the exponentiation you know from the Powers, roots lesson.
prop.interestIntro2: Inflation is the same thing backwards: if prices rise by 10% a year, the same money buys less and less each year. Set the rate and the years and compare what compound interest gives with what you would get if only the original amount earned interest every year.
prop.interestDef1: Interest: the amount a bank pays for the money kept there (or the amount asked for a loan). Interest rate: the interest as a percentage, counted for one year.
prop.interestDef2: Inflation: the general rise of prices. At 10% inflation a year, what costs 10 000 Ft today will cost 11 000 Ft in a year, so the same money is worth less.
prop.interestGap: Over {{years}} years compound interest gives {{diff}} Ft more than simple interest.
prop.interestInflation: What you buy for {{amount}} Ft today will cost {{future}} Ft in {{years}} years, so today’s {{amount}} Ft will then be worth only {{power}} Ft.
prop.interestTask: You put 200 000 Ft in the bank at 4% a year. How much money will you have after two years?
prop.interestHint: Multiply by 1.04 twice, not by 1.08 once.

lin.stepMoveNum: Move the numbers to the right.
