lin.balanceIntro1: Picture a balance scale in equilibrium. On the left there are three identical boxes of unknown weight and two one-kilo weights, on the right one box and eight kilos. Take a box off both sides and the scale stays balanced. Take two kilos off both sides and it stays balanced too. That is the balance principle, and it is exactly how an equation is solved.
lin.balanceDef: The balance principle: if we do the same thing to both sides of an equation — add or subtract the same amount, multiply or divide by the same number other than zero — the solution of the equation does not change. That is how an equation is brought step by step to a simpler form, until nothing is left but x = a number.
lin.balanceIntro2: The goal is to leave a single box on one side and nothing else: then the other side tells you what it weighs. Try the moves — only the ones that can be made on both sides at once are on offer.
lin.balanceAria: A balance scale in equilibrium. The equation right now: {{equation}}.
lin.balanceWhyDisabled: A greyed-out move cannot be made right now: only moves that work on both sides at once are allowed.
lin.balanceStepRemoveX: Took one box off both sides.
lin.balanceSolved: One box weighs {{x}} kg. Check: 3 · {{x}} + 2 = {{x}} + 8 — both sides come to {{left}}.
lin.balanceHint: Subtract 2x from both sides, add 7 to both sides, then divide both sides by 3.
lin.setsIntro1: Not every equation has one solution. The equation 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 is true for every number, because the two sides are the same expression — that is an identity. The equation x + 1 = x + 2 is true for no number at all. The solution of 2x + 5 = 8 is one and a half — but if the problem is about a number of children, one and a half is not an answer.
lin.setsDef1: Base set: the set of numbers among which we look for the solution of the equation. If the problem does not say, the base set is the real numbers; if it is about a count of things, it is the natural numbers.
lin.setsDef2: Solution set: the set of those elements of the base set that make the equation true. It may be a single number, it may be empty, and it may be the whole base set.
lin.setsIntro2: So an equation always comes with the question of which numbers are in play at all. Pick an equation and a base set, and watch how the solution set changes.
lin.setsNatNote: Here 0 counts as a natural number too.
lin.setsAllExpand: The left side is 2(x + 3), which expands to 2x + 6: the two sides are the same expression, written two ways.
lin.setsAllNote: True for every x: the solution set is the whole base set.
lin.setsNoneNote: True for no x at all: the solution set is empty.
lin.setsVerdict_single: x = {{x}} lies in the base set, so the solution set is this one number.
lin.setsVerdict_outside: x = {{x}} is not {{noun}}, so over this base set there is no solution.
lin.setsVerdict_all: The equation is true for every number, so the solution set is the whole base set: {{base}}.
lin.setsVerdict_none: The two sides are never equal, so the solution set is empty — whatever the base set is.
lin.setsTask: What is the solution set of 2x + 7 = 4 if the base set is Z?
lin.setsHint: Solve the equation first: x = −1.5. Then ask whether that is an integer.
lin.graphIntro1: The two sides of an equation are two separate expressions, and both can be drawn: y = x + 1 is one line, y = −x + 7 the other. Where the two lines cross, the two sides are equal — the x-coordinate of the crossing point is the solution of the equation.
lin.graphRule: Graphical solution: draw the graphs of y = left side and y = right side; the x-coordinate of the crossing point is the solution.
lin.graphIntro2: Move the two lines and watch the crossing point. If the lines are parallel there is no crossing point, so there is no solution. If they coincide, every point is common: an identity. The picture also shows what the arithmetic does not: roughly where the solution is, before you have taken a single step.
lin.graphIntro3: A drawing on a computer is quick and vivid, but it can only be read approximately: if the crossing point is at x = 2.33, the picture will not tell you that it is exactly 7/3. So the picture is for estimating and for checking; the exact solution comes from the balance principle.
lin.graphResult_one: The crossing point: x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}. That is the solution of the equation.
lin.graphResult_none: The two lines are parallel: no common point, no solution.
lin.graphResult_all: The two lines coincide: every x is a solution.
lin.graphTask: Read it off the picture: where do the two lines cross? Give the solution.
lin.graphHint: Look for the x where both lines are at the same height.
lin.ineqTitle: 4. Inequalities: the balance principle with one exception
lin.ineqIntro1: 3 < 5, that is true. Multiply both sides by −1: −3 and −5. Which is bigger? −3. So −3 > −5: the sign has turned around. For inequalities the balance principle works almost exactly as it does for equations, with a single exception: if you multiply or divide by a negative number, the relation sign has to be turned around.
lin.ineqDef: Solution set of an inequality: the set of those elements of the base set for which the inequality is true. For a linear inequality it is a half-line on the number line: every number above or below one bound, with the bound taken along or left out.
lin.ineqRule: The sign turns around if you multiply or divide both sides of an inequality by a negative number. Multiplying by a positive number, or adding and subtracting anything, leaves it as it is.
lin.ineqIntro2: The solution here is not one number but a whole range, so we draw it on a number line. And there is a check that is always worth making: pick a number from the range, put it into the original inequality, and see whether it comes out true. If you forgot to turn the sign around, this shows it immediately.
lin.ineqLineTitle: The solution on the number line
lin.ineqLineAria: Number line: the solution is the half-line x {{rel}} {{bound}}, with the test point on it.
lin.ineqForget: What if we forgot to turn the sign?
lin.ineqForgetNote: The half-line in the second colour is the wrong answer. Drag the test point onto it: it says something different from the original inequality.
lin.ineqNoFlipHere: In this example we divide by a positive number, so the sign stays — there is nothing to get wrong here.
lin.ineqTrue: true, so {{x}} is in the solution set.
lin.ineqFalse: false, so {{x}} is not in the solution set.
lin.ineqHint: Try x = 0 in the original: 5 ≥ −4 is true, so 0 must be in the solution set.
lin.systemsIntro1: Two numbers add up to 10 and differ by 4. Which two numbers are they? There are two unknowns, so two equations are needed: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. One equation on its own is not enough — x + y = 10 has infinitely many solutions — but the two together pick out exactly one pair.
lin.systemsDef: System of equations: several equations sharing the same unknowns, all of which have to hold at once. Its solution is the pair (x; y) that makes every one of them true.
lin.systemsIntro2: There are two methods, and both come to the same thing: make one unknown disappear so that a one-unknown equation is left. With substitution you express one unknown from one equation and write it into the other. With equal coefficients you multiply the equations so that the coefficients of one unknown become opposites, then add the two equations. Pick a method and step through it.
lin.systemsShopText: Three pens and two notebooks cost 1900 Ft, one pen and one notebook cost 800 Ft. x is the price of a pen, y the price of a notebook.
lin.systemsResult: The solution is x = {{x}}, y = {{y}}, and this pair makes both equations true. The other method leads to exactly the same place.
lin.systemsTask: Two numbers add up to 12 and differ by 2. Which two numbers are they?
lin.systemsHint: Add the two equations: y drops out and 2x = 14 is left.
lin.sysgraphIntro1: An equation in two unknowns, x + y = 5 say, is a line in the coordinate system: every point of it is a solution (x; y). Two equations are two lines, and the solution of the system is the point that lies on both of them — the crossing point.
lin.sysgraphIntro2: This also makes the three possibilities plain. Two lines either cross at one point (one solution), or are parallel (no solution), or coincide (infinitely many solutions). Pick one of the three systems.
lin.sysgraphRule: Three cases: crossing lines — one solution; parallel lines — no solution; coincident lines — infinitely many solutions.
lin.sysgraphResult_none: The two lines are parallel: they have no common point, so the system has no solution.
lin.sysgraphResult_infinite: The two lines coincide: every point is common to both, so the system has infinitely many solutions.
lin.sysgraphDigital: On a computer you can read the crossing point off the screen, but only approximately; the exact pair comes from the methods of section 5. The picture is good for seeing in advance which of the three cases you are dealing with.
lin.sysgraphHint: Substitute the pair into both equations: both of them have to come out true.
lin.modelIntro1: Two towns are 180 km apart. A car sets off from one of them at 60 km/h, and at the same moment another car sets off from the other at 30 km/h, towards it. When do they meet? There is not a single equation in the text — we have to write it. This is modelling, and it has five steps.
lin.modelDef: Mathematical model: the word problem translated into the language of mathematics — the data, the unknown, and the relation between them written as an equation. We do the arithmetic in the model, but the answer is always given back in terms of the original situation, and we check that it makes sense there.
lin.modelSteps: The five steps: 1. gather the data, 2. choose the unknown, 3. write the equation, 4. solve it, 5. check it against the original text and answer.
lin.modelIntro2: Gathering the data: 180 km, 60 km/h, 30 km/h. Choosing the unknown: let t be the time elapsed, in hours. The equation: in t hours the first car covers 60t km and the second 30t km; they meet when those two together make up the 180 km: 60t + 30t = 180. Solving: t = 2. Checking and answering: in 2 hours 120 + 60 = 180 km, so they meet after two hours. Drag the time and watch the picture and the equation meet.
lin.modelAria: A road from 0 to 180 km: after {{t}} hours the first car is at {{car1}} km and the second at {{car2}} km.
lin.modelLine: t = {{t}} hours: 60 · {{t}} + 30 · {{t}} = {{sum}} km, still {{gap}} km short of the 180.
lin.modelMet: t = 2 hours: 120 + 60 = 180 km — they have met. That is the solution of the equation.
lin.modelPassed: t = {{t}} hours: they have already passed each other, together they have covered {{sum}} km. More than the 180 km is not a sensible answer to the question.
lin.modelTask: The same problem, but the second car goes at 40 km/h. After how many hours do they meet?
lin.modelHint: Write the equation the same way: 60t + 40t = 180.
lin.problemsTitle: 8. Joint work, mixtures, money — and faulty data
lin.problemsIntro1: The same five steps work in other situations too; only the relation is different. For joint work we add up how much of the job each of them does in an hour. For mixing we add up the amount of the dissolved substance, not the percentages. For money we are often given only a total and a difference. Pick a problem and use the slider to find the value where the two sides agree — then look at how the equation gives the same thing.
lin.problemsWorkRule: Joint work: if alone they finish in t₁ and t₂ hours, together they finish in t hours, where t/t₁ + t/t₂ = 1.
lin.problemsMixRule: Mixing: the dissolved substance does not go anywhere: the amounts in the parts add up to the amount in the mixture.
lin.workText: Anna paints a room in 6 hours, Bence in 3. How long does it take the two of them together?
lin.workDone: t = 2 hours: 1/3 + 2/3 = 1, the room is done. That is the solution of the equation.
lin.mixText: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution, and we have a 20% and a 50% one. How much should we take of the 20% one?
lin.mixLine: x = {{x}} l: 0.2 · {{x}} + 0.5 · {{rest}} = {{amount}} l of substance, which is {{pct}}%.
lin.mixDone: x = 2 l: 0.4 + 2 = 2.4 litres of substance in 6 litres, which is exactly 40%. That is the solution of the equation.
lin.moneyText: Two bills come to 30 000 Ft together, one of them 4000 Ft more than the other. How much is each of them?
lin.moneyDone: 13 000 + 17 000 = 30 000 Ft, and the difference is 4000 Ft. The two bills are 13 000 Ft and 17 000 Ft.
lin.problemsIntro2: Finally, an important skill: noticing when a text does not add up. Sometimes a datum is missing and the equation cannot be written at all. Sometimes there is more data than needed, but it does no harm. And sometimes the extra datum contradicts the rest — then the problem has no solution, and that has to be said out loud rather than covered up with an invented number.
lin.data_v1: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution. We have a 20% one and a stronger one. How much should we take of the 20% one?
lin.data_v2: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution, and we have a 20% and a 50% one. The solutions cost 300 Ft a litre. How much should we take of the 20% one?
lin.data_v3: We need 6 litres of a 40% solution, so we pour together 3 litres of the 20% one and 4 litres of the 50% one. What will the strength of the mixture be?

quad.introTitle: 1. The quadratic equation and equivalent transformations
quad.introIntro1: The square of a number is 5 more than four times the number. Which number is it? If x is the number, then x² = 4x + 5. In this equation the unknown appears squared, so the balance principle on its own is not enough: subtract and divide all you like, the x² will not go away. New methods are needed, and that is what this lesson is about.
quad.introDef1: Quadratic equation: an equation that can be brought to the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b and c are given numbers and a ≠ 0. Here a is the coefficient of x², b is the coefficient of x, and c is the constant term.
quad.introDef2: Equivalent transformation: a step after which the equation has the same solution set. Every move of the balance principle is one: adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing by a number other than zero, expanding brackets. Dividing by an expression that contains the unknown is not (a root can be lost), and neither is squaring (a false root can appear), so after those you have to check.
quad.introIntro2: The first step is always the same: move everything to one side so that zero is left on the other, and order the terms by their power. This way every quadratic equation takes the form ax² + bx + c = 0, and the three numbers a, b and c tell you everything about it. Pick an equation and watch how it turns into that form.
quad.introIntro3: And one important rule along the way: we may only take steps that do not change the solutions. It is tempting to divide x² = 4x by x, and out comes x = 4 — but 0 was a solution too, and it was lost, because dividing by zero is not allowed. The right way is factoring: x(x − 4) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 4.
quad.introLostTitle: Why can't we divide by x?
quad.introCheck: Check: 0² = 4 · 0 is true, 4² = 4 · 4 is true — both are roots.
quad.introTask: Bring it to zero-ordered form: 3x² = 5 − 2x. What are a, b and c?
quad.introHint: Move everything to the left; a term that moves across changes sign.
quad.factorIntro1: The left-hand side of x² − 5x + 6 = 0 can be written as a product: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. And a product is zero only if one of its factors is zero, so x = 2 or x = 3. This is the quickest method whenever we can find the two numbers: we are looking for a pair whose product is 6 and whose sum is 5.
quad.factorDef: Root-factor form: writing a quadratic expression with its roots: ax² + bx + c = a(x − x₁)(x − x₂), where x₁ and x₂ are the roots of the equation. If the equation has no root, it has no such form either.
quad.factorRule: A product is zero if and only if at least one of its factors is zero.
quad.factorIntro2: It works backwards too. If you know the roots, you can write the equation: the equation with roots 2 and 3 is (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, which expands to x² − 5x + 6 = 0. Set the two roots and watch the coefficients follow: the middle term is the opposite of their sum, the last one is their product.
quad.factorResult: Sum: {{sum}} = {{sumValue}}, so b = {{b}}. Product: {{prod}} = {{prodValue}}, so c = {{c}}.
quad.factorCrossNote: The curve crosses the horizontal axis at exactly the two roots.
quad.factorFindTitle: The other way round: find the two numbers
quad.factorFindNote: The two numbers whose sum is −b and whose product is c: those are the roots.
quad.factorZeroC: If c = 0, x can be taken out: one of the roots is 0.
quad.factorDiffSq: If b = 0, it is a difference of two squares.
quad.factorHint: Look for two numbers whose product is 12 and whose sum is 7.
quad.completeIntro1: Not every equation can be factored in your head. The left-hand side of x² + 6x + 5 = 0, however, can be completed to a square, the way we learned with algebraic expressions: (x + 3)² − 4 = 0, that is (x + 3)² = 4. That is easy now: whatever has 4 as its square is 2 or −2. So x + 3 = 2 or x + 3 = −2, that is x = −1 or x = −5.
quad.completeRule: When a square equals a number: if (something)² = k, then something = √k or something = −√k when k > 0; something = 0 when k = 0; and there is no solution when k < 0.
quad.completeIntro2: This method also shows straight away how many solutions there are. If the square equals a positive number, there are two roots. If it equals zero, there is one — the two roots coincide. If it equals a negative number, there is none, because a square cannot be negative. Set the two numbers and see which case comes out.
quad.completeResult_two: The right-hand side is {{k}} > 0: two roots.
quad.completeResult_one: The right-hand side is 0: a single root.
quad.completeResult_none: The right-hand side is {{k}} < 0: no solution.
quad.completeTask: Solve by completing the square: x² − 4x − 12 = 0.
quad.formulaIntro1: You do not have to complete the square from scratch for every equation. Do it once on the general equation ax² + bx + c = 0 and you get a formula you only have to write the three numbers into. That is the quadratic formula. Below, the derivation runs in two columns: letters on the left, the same step on a concrete equation on the right, so you can see that the formula does exactly what you would do.
quad.formulaDef1: The quadratic formula: the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 are x₁,₂ = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a). The ± sign means we calculate once with a plus and once with a minus: that is what gives the two roots.
quad.formulaDef2: Discriminant: the expression under the root sign, D = b² − 4ac. If D > 0 there are two different roots; if D = 0 there is one (double) root; if D < 0 there is no real root.
quad.formulaIntro2: The number b² − 4ac under the root sign has a name of its own, because it decides how many roots there are: positive means two, zero means one, negative means none — the same three cases as in the previous section.
quad.parDivideOne: Divide by a — here a = 1, so nothing changes.
quad.parFormula: Subtract the b/2a term: this is the quadratic formula.
quad.parNoRoot: A square cannot be negative: no real root.
quad.formulaSubTitle: The formula with the three numbers in it
quad.formulaHistory: The Babylonians could already solve quadratic equations; the modern shape of the formula is the work of al-Khwarizmi in the 9th century and of the Renaissance mathematicians. The formula for the cubic was found by Tartaglia and Cardano in the 1500s, and the one for the quartic by Ferrari. From the fifth degree on there is no such formula: Abel proved that in 1824, and Galois showed why. A good topic for a short talk.
quad.formulaHint: D = 25 − 16 = 9, its root is 3, and the denominator is 2 · 2.
quad.discIntro1: Draw the function y = ax² + bx + c: you get a parabola. The roots of the equation are where the parabola crosses the x axis, because that is where y = 0. So the three cases show up in the picture too: the parabola crosses the axis twice, touches it once, or never reaches it.
quad.discRule: D and the parabola: D > 0 — two crossings; D = 0 — the parabola touches the x axis; D < 0 — the parabola never reaches the x axis.
quad.discIntro2: Set the three coefficients and watch the discriminant and the picture at the same time. If a is positive the parabola opens upwards, if it is negative it opens downwards. The c tells you where it crosses the y axis. The roots can only be read off the picture approximately, and the exact value comes from the formula — but the picture tells you at once how many roots to look for, and roughly where.
quad.discReadNote: The roots in the picture: where the curve passes through the horizontal axis.
quad.discNoRoot: The parabola never reaches the x axis, so the equation has no real root.
quad.discTask: For which c does x² + 4x + c = 0 have exactly one root?
quad.discHint: One root means D = 0, that is 16 − 4c = 0.
quad.ineqIntro1: When is x² − x − 6 negative? The question is an inequality: x² − x − 6 < 0. The best answer comes from the picture. The roots of the parabola are −2 and 3, and between the two roots the parabola is below the x axis, outside them above it. So x² − x − 6 < 0 exactly when −2 < x < 3.
quad.ineqRule: An upward parabola (a > 0) is negative between its two roots and positive outside them. If it has no root, it is positive everywhere.
quad.ineqIntro2: The recipe: find the roots, draw the parabola, and read off which stretch is on the right side. Then check with a test point: 0 lies between the two roots, and 0² − 0 − 6 = −6 really is negative. Pick an inequality and try several points.
quad.ineqLineTitle: The solution on the number line
quad.ineqLineAria: Number line: the solution set is {{set}}, with the test point on it.
quad.ineqSet_between: Between the two roots the parabola is below the axis.
quad.ineqSet_outside: Outside the two roots the parabola is above the axis.
quad.ineqSet_allBut: The parabola touches the axis: it is positive everywhere except at one place.
quad.ineqSet_none: The parabola never reaches the axis, so there is no solution.
quad.ineqSet_all: The parabola is on the right side everywhere: every number is a solution.
quad.ineqSet_only: A single number is the solution: where the parabola touches the axis.
quad.ineqTrue: true, it is in the solution set.
quad.ineqFalse: false, it is not in the solution set.
quad.ineqHint: The roots are −2 and 2. Try x = 0 and x = 3.
quad.reduceTitle: 7. Equations that reduce to a quadratic
quad.reduceIntro1: The equation x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 is of the fourth degree, yet our tools can solve it, because only x² and x⁴ appear in it. Let us call x² by the name u: u² − 5u + 4 = 0, which is a quadratic, with roots u = 1 and u = 4. At the end we come back to x: x² = 1 gives x = ±1, x² = 4 gives x = ±2. Four roots, out of a single quadratic equation.
quad.reduceDef: Introducing a new unknown (substitution): we name a repeated part of the equation with a single letter, solve the simpler equation we get, then work the original unknown back out of the values found — dropping, along the way, the values that the substituted expression can never take.
quad.reduceIntro2: Coming back needs care: u = x² is never negative, so if the value we get for u is negative, no x belongs to it. This is the range check: we ask what values the thing we substituted can take at all. Step through the three examples.
quad.reduceRejectNote: One of the u values was dropped: x² is never negative.
quad.reduceTask: How many real roots does x⁴ − 10x² + 9 = 0 have?
quad.reduceHint: The roots for u are 1 and 9, and every positive u gives two x.
quad.wordTitle: 8. Word problems: which root is the answer?
quad.wordIntro1: One side of a rectangular garden is 3 metres longer than the other, and its area is 40 m². How long are its sides? Let x be the shorter side: x(x + 3) = 40, which rearranges to x² + 3x − 40 = 0. The roots are 5 and −8. Mathematically −8 is a root, but a side cannot be negative, so the answer is 5 m and 8 m. In word problems this is the most important step: of the roots, only the one that makes sense in the original situation counts.
quad.wordSteps: The five steps for a quadratic: the data, the unknown, the equation, the solution — and at the end the filtering of the roots: which one gives a sensible answer to the original question?
quad.wordIntro2: The same thing in physics: the height of a ball thrown upwards after t seconds is h = 20t − 5t² metres. When does it hit the ground? h = 0, that is 20t − 5t² = 0, 5t(4 − t) = 0, so t = 0 or t = 4. The 0 is the moment of the throw, and landing happens at t = 4. Here the parabola is not just a drawing: it is the flight of the ball over time. Drag the slider in both problems.
quad.wordGardenAria: A rectangular garden: its shorter side is {{x}} metres, the longer one {{long}} metres, and its area is {{area}} square metres.
quad.gardenLine: x = {{x}} m, so the area is {{x}} · {{long}} = {{area}} m².
quad.gardenDone: x = 5 m: 5 · 8 = 40 m². That is the answer: 5 m and 8 m.
quad.gardenReject: −8 is a root as well, but a side cannot be negative, so we drop it.
quad.ballLine: t = {{t}} s, and then h = {{h}} m.
quad.ballDone: t = 4 s: h = 0, the ball has landed.
quad.ballBelow: Beyond t = 4 the formula gives a negative height, but the ball is already on the ground — the model no longer holds here.
quad.ballStart: t = 0 is the moment of the throw, so the answer is t = 4.
quad.wordTask: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 56. Which two numbers are they?
quad.wordHint: The equation is x(x + 1) = 56, and one of the roots is negative.

fn.assignTitle: 1. Assignments: exactly one arrow, and one-to-one
fn.assignIntro1: To every student we assign their shoe size. To every country its capital. To every person their siblings. All three are assignments, but they are not alike. With shoe sizes every student gets exactly one number, and two students may get the same one. With capitals every country gets exactly one city, and no two countries share a capital. With siblings there are people who get none and people who get two.
fn.assignDef1: Assignment: to the elements of one set we assign elements of another, drawn as arrows, say. The first set is the base set, the second is the image set.
fn.assignDef2: Single-valued assignment: every element of the base set gets exactly one element — exactly one arrow leaves every node. A single-valued assignment is called a function.
fn.assignDef3: One-to-one assignment: it is single-valued, and on top of that no element of the image set receives more than one arrow. Then the arrows can be turned around, and the assignment stays single-valued that way too.
fn.assignIntro2: In mathematics only the first two count as functions: the ones where every element gets exactly one other. Pick an example and move the arrows about — the card tells you the moment being single-valued breaks down.
fn.assignAria: Arrow diagram: {{scenario}}. The base set on the left, the image set on the right.
fn.assignSelectAria: Where should the arrow from {{node}} point?
fn.assignVerdict_function: Single-valued, so it is a function — but not one-to-one: two arrows arrive at the node {{node}}.
fn.assignVerdict_oneToOne: One-to-one: exactly one arrow leaves every node, and at most one arrives at any node.
fn.assignTask: What kind of assignment is it? Decide for all four.
fn.quiz_plate: to every car its number plate
fn.assignHint: Ask the two questions: does everyone get exactly one? And can two of them get the same one?
fn.defineTitle: 2. Giving a function: domain, range, substitution value
fn.defineIntro1: A taxi charges 700 forints for setting off and 300 forints per kilometre. The fare therefore depends on the distance: f(x) = 300x + 700, where x is the number of kilometres. This is a function: the rule says what we assign to every x. Which x-es are allowed has to be stated separately — here we look at 0 to 10 km.
fn.defineDef1: Function: a single-valued assignment between a base set and an image set. The notation f(x) means the value the function f assigns to x.
fn.defineDef2: Domain: the set of those x values the function assigns something to. If the problem does not say, it contains every number the formula makes sense for.
fn.defineDef3: Image set and range: the image set is the set the values come from (the real numbers, say); the range is the set of the values the function actually takes. The range is a part of the image set.
fn.defineDef4: Substitution value: the number the function assigns to a given x, obtained by substituting that x into the formula. f(3) = 300 · 3 + 700 = 1600.
fn.defineIntro2: Pick a function, then click the x values: the card works out the substitution value, writes it into the table and draws the point. Once all the points are up, you can see the whole function. The formula, the table and the graph all say the same thing, only differently.
fn.defineAria: Points on a pair of axes: {{rule}}, {{n}} points worked out so far.
fn.defineRange: Domain: {{domain}}. Values worked out so far: {{values}}.
fn.defineBackTitle: The other way round: which x gets a given value?
fn.defineBackAria: Which value are you looking for the x of?
fn.defineBackNone: f(x) = {{y}} holds for no x at all: this value is not in the range.
fn.defineTask: f(x) = 3x − 5. Which x does it assign 7 to?
fn.readIntro1: The temperature of a winter day, hour by hour: at 4 in the morning it was coldest at −4 degrees, at 2 in the afternoon warmest at 8 degrees, and at 7 in the morning and 11 at night it was exactly 0. A graph tells you all that at a glance — once you know what to look for.
fn.readDef1: Zero: an x where the value of the function is 0 — the graph crosses or touches the x axis there.
fn.readDef2: Extremum: the largest value of the function is its maximum, the smallest its minimum. The place of the maximum is the x where it is taken; the maximum itself is the value.
fn.readDef3: Increasing and decreasing: a function is increasing on a stretch if a larger x gets a larger value (the graph climbs from left to right), and decreasing if a larger x gets a smaller value (the graph descends).
fn.readIntro2: The buttons highlight the properties one at a time: where the curve crosses the horizontal axis, where its highest and lowest points are, which stretch it rises on and which it falls on. And the slider reads off the temperature for any hour you like.
fn.read_zeros: Zeros: {{list}}. This is where the curve crosses the horizontal axis.
fn.read_up: Increasing: {{spans}}. The graph climbs from left to right here.
fn.read_down: Decreasing: {{spans}}. The graph descends from left to right here.
fn.readTask: On which interval is the function increasing?
fn.readHint: Follow the curve from left to right and see which stretch it climbs on.
fn.linearIntro1: A taxi fare, a phone bill, a temperature in Fahrenheit — all the same shape of formula: a number times x, plus another number. f(x) = mx + b. Its graph is always a straight line, and both numbers can be read off it: b is where the line crosses the y axis, and m is how much it climbs for one step to the right.
fn.linearDef1: Linear function: a function of the form f(x) = mx + b, where m and b are given numbers. Its graph is a straight line. If m = 0, the function is constant.
fn.linearDef2: Slope and intercept: m is the slope — this is how much the value changes when x grows by one; b is the intercept — the value at x = 0, where the line crosses the y axis.
fn.linearIntro2: Set the two numbers and watch the step on the picture: one unit right, m units up. If m is negative the line goes down, if m = 0 it is horizontal. Then the other way round: read the two numbers off a picture — that is the exercise.
fn.linearResult: b = {{b}}: this is where the line crosses the y axis. m = {{m}}: for one step to the right it {{dir}} by {{step}} units.
fn.linearResultFlat: b = {{b}}: this is where the line crosses the y axis. m = 0: the line is horizontal, every x gets the same value.
fn.linearWhyB: This is b: the value at x = 0.
fn.linearWhyM: One step to the right: the value changed by m.
fn.linearTask: The line passes through (0; −1) and (2; 3). What are m and b?
fn.linearHint: b is the value at x = 0. m is the change in y divided by the change in x between the two points.
fn.elemIntro1: Three functions are worth knowing thoroughly, because they keep coming back: the square function, the square root function and the function of inverse proportion. Each has a different shape, a different domain, and behaves differently as x grows.
fn.elemDef1: Square function: f(x) = x², its domain is all the real numbers and its range the non-negative ones. Its graph is a parabola, its minimum is 0 at x = 0; it decreases for x < 0 and increases for x > 0.
fn.elemDef2: Square root function: f(x) = √x, defined only for x ≥ 0, its values are non-negative. It increases throughout, its minimum is 0 at x = 0, and it has no maximum.
fn.elemDef3: The function of inverse proportion: f(x) = 1/x, defined for every x except 0, and its value is never 0. It has neither a zero nor an extremum; its graph has two branches (a hyperbola) and decreases on both of them.
fn.elemIntro2: Pick one and read its properties off the table. Moving the horizontal line with the slider also shows how many x-es a given value belongs to: that is the number of solutions of the equation f(x) = c. For x², say, 4 belongs to two x-es (2 and −2), 0 to one, and −1 to none.
fn.elemSolutions_0: f(x) = {{c}}: no solution — the line never reaches the curve.
fn.elemSolutions_1: f(x) = {{c}}: one solution, x = {{x1}}. The line meets the curve in one place.
fn.elemSolutions_2: f(x) = {{c}}: two solutions, x = {{x1}} and x = {{x2}}. The line meets the curve in two places.
fn.elemHint: A zero is where the graph touches the x axis. Which graph never gets there?
fn.transformIntro1: If you know the graph of x², you know the graph of (x − 3)² + 2 as well: the same parabola, only moved. There are four basic steps, and each is one movement on the picture: adding at the end of the formula shifts up and down, adding next to the x shifts left and right, multiplying stretches or squashes, and the absolute value folds whatever was below the axis up above it.
fn.transformRule: f(x) + c: shifts up by c (down for a negative c). f(x + c): shifts left by c (right for a negative c). c · f(x): stretches by a factor of c in the y direction; a negative c reflects in the x axis. |f(x)|: whatever was below the axis comes up above it.
fn.transformIntro2: One thing goes against your first instinct: the graph of f(x + 3) shifts to the left, not to the right. Think it through: f(x + 3) takes at x = −3 the value f takes at 0 — so everything happens 3 earlier. Try it with the sliders; the dashed curve is the original.

fn.transformTask: Which formula gives the graph of x² shifted 3 to the right?
fn.transformHint: The lowest point of the new graph is at x = 3. Which formula gives 0 there?
fn.inverseIntro1: Celsius becomes Fahrenheit like this: f(x) = 1.8x + 32. And backwards? If we know the Fahrenheit, we get the Celsius by doing the steps in reverse: subtract 32, divide by 1.8. That is the inverse assignment. Only a one-to-one assignment can be turned around, because otherwise one value would belong to several x-es and we would not know which to choose.
fn.inverseDef: Inverse assignment: the inverse of a one-to-one assignment f is the assignment that gives back x for every value f(x). Its graph is the mirror image of the graph of f in the line y = x.
fn.inverseIntro2: On the picture the turning around is a reflection: the graph of the inverse is the mirror image of the original in the line y = x, because every point (x; y) becomes (y; x). Drag the slider and watch the point and its mirror image. The whole of x² cannot be turned around — 4 belongs to both 2 and −2 — but if we look only at x ≥ 0, its inverse is exactly √x.
fn.inverseChartNote: The two curves are mirror images of each other in the dashed line y = x. The picture shows only the stretch where both of them fit.
fn.inverseSquareTitle: Why can x² not be turned around?
fn.inverseSquareNote: 4 belongs to both 2 and −2, so it is not one-to-one. If we look only at x ≥ 0, every value occurs once and its inverse is √x — which is why the root function lives only on the non-negative numbers.
fn.inverseTask: f(x) = 2x + 6. What does the inverse assignment assign to 10?
fn.modelTitle: 8. Functions in practice: distance–time and the largest area
fn.modelIntro1: You set off from home in the morning: 6 minutes walking to the stop (400 m), 4 minutes waiting for the bus, 8 minutes on the bus covering 2 km, 4 minutes standing at the lights, and finally a 3-minute walk to school. A distance–time graph tells the whole story: time on the horizontal axis, the distance from home on the vertical one. Where the line is flat you are standing still; the steeper it is, the faster you are going.
fn.modelRule: On a distance–time graph the slope is the speed: a flat stretch means standing still, a steeper stretch means going faster.
fn.modelIntro2: The second task is a classic: you fence off a rectangle with 20 metres of string. Which sides make the area largest? If one side is x, the other is 10 − x, and the area is x(10 − x). That is a quadratic function, its graph is a downward parabola, and its largest value is at the vertex. Drag the slider and find it.

deriv.title: The derivative: a secant becoming a tangent
deriv.intro1: The derivative answers one question: how steep is the curve at a single point x₀? Think of the curve as a hill you are walking on — the derivative is the slope of the ground exactly under your feet.
deriv.intro2: There's a problem, though. Slope means "rise over run", and that needs two points. One point has no rise and no run. So we cheat in three steps:
deriv.steps12: 1. Pick a second point a small distance h away, at x₀+h. 2. Draw the straight line through both points — the orange secant — and measure its slope, which is just rise over run:
deriv.step3: 3. Shrink h. As the second point slides toward the first, the secant tips over into the dashed tangent — the line that just grazes the curve. The derivative is defined as the value this slope settles on:
deriv.dragNote: Drag the h slider toward 0 and watch it happen. The numbers under the chart update live with your slider.
deriv.texLimitHeading: the limit it is heading for:
deriv.noTangent: No tangent here! Coming from the right the slopes settle on {{right}}, but coming from the left they settle on {{left}}. The two sides disagree, so there is no single answer and f′({{x0}}) does not exist. The curve has a corner at this point.
deriv.tableTitle: The limit, computed like a math student
deriv.tableIntro: "Limit as h approaches 0" sounds abstract, but you can't actually set h = 0 — that would divide by zero. A limit is a promise instead: the closer h gets to 0, the closer the slope gets to one particular number. On paper that promise is just a table. Halve h again and again and watch the right-hand column stop changing. The number it settles on is the derivative.
deriv.tryIt: Try it: pick |x| and slide x₀ to 0. The table refuses to settle, because approaching from the right gives +1 and from the left gives −1 (tick the checkbox to compare the two directions). A corner has no single steepness — that is exactly what "the limit does not exist" means. Then try sin(x) at x₀ = 0 and watch the quotients march to exactly 1: the sine curve leaves the origin at 45°.

integ.title: The integral: rectangles becoming area
integ.intro1: The integral answers: how much area sits between the curve and the x-axis, from a to b? For a rectangle that's easy — width times height. But a curved roof has no ready-made area formula. So, just like with the derivative, we cheat with straight edges, in three steps:
integ.step1: 1. Cut the stretch from a to b into n equal strips. Each strip has width
integ.step2: 2. On each strip, stand a rectangle. Its height is the curve's value at one chosen spot in the strip (the left edge, the middle, or the right edge — your choice above). Rectangles we can measure: each one contributes height × width, and adding all n of them gives the Riemann sum:
integ.step3: 3. Use more, thinner strips. The error lives in the little slivers between the flat rectangle tops and the curve, and thinner strips leave smaller slivers. The integral is the value the total settles on — and the ∫ symbol is literally a stretched-out S, for "sum":
integ.dragNote: Drag n up and watch the orange rectangles melt into the blue area. The numbers under the chart track your sliders.
integ.texLimitHeading: the limit it is heading for:
integ.degenerate: a and b coincide — the area of a zero-width region is 0. Drag them apart.
integ.tableTitle: The limit again, as a table
integ.tableIntro: Same move as on the Derivative tab: a limit is a promise that the numbers settle, and a table makes the promise visible. Each row doubles the number of rectangles. Read down the third column and watch it stop changing — the value it locks onto is the integral.
integ.tryIt: Try it: switch "left edge" to "midpoint" and watch the table settle dramatically faster. Sampling in the middle of each strip lets the rectangle's overshoot on one side cancel its undershoot on the other. Integrate sin(x) from −2 to 2 and get 0: area below the axis counts as negative, and the two halves cancel exactly. And try |x| — the corner that broke the derivative gives the integral no trouble at all, because adding areas doesn't care about a kink the way slopes do. That one-sidedness is why the fundamental theorem of calculus — the statement that derivative and integral undo each other — is a real theorem someone had to prove, not an obvious fact.

fft.subtitle: The Fourier transform's claim: any repeating signal is secretly a sum of simple waves. This page lets you test the claim. Type a function, and the app measures it at N points, finds which waves hide inside (the FFT), throws away all but the strongest ones, and rebuilds the signal from what's left (the inverse FFT). If the rebuilt curve still matches, a few waves were enough to carry the whole signal.
fft.keepLabel: Strongest components to keep (zero-amplitude bins are skipped): {{n}}
fft.timeNote: The blue curve is your function, measured at N points. The dashed orange curve is the rebuilt version — the inverse FFT of only the kept components. Where the two hug each other, those few waves already tell the whole story; drag the "components" slider down and watch the orange curve lose detail first, then shape.
fft.waveNote: Here are the hidden waves the FFT found, drawn one per row so you can see each ingredient on its own — strongest first, all on the same y-scale so heights are comparable. Each label gives the wave's recipe: strength × cos(speed × x + head start). Add every row together, point by point, and you get exactly the dashed orange curve above.
fft.freqNote: The same information as a bar chart — the signal's "recipe card". One bar per possible frequency (bin k = 0 … N/2): its position says how fast that wave repeats, its height says how strongly it is present. Most bars are near zero because most frequencies simply aren't in the signal. Hover a bar for its exact frequency, amplitude and phase; click one to see its value computed step by step below.
fft.binNote: Pick a bin with the +/− buttons, or click any bar in the spectrum above, and watch its value worked out by hand.
fft.resultNote: The recipe in one line — this sum of simple waves is what the inverse FFT actually draws as the dashed curve. The RMS error above says how far that drawing is from your function, averaged over all sample points (0 means a perfect match).

bin.intro: A "bin" is one slot of the transform's output. Bin k asks a single question: how much of the signal is a wave that repeats exactly {{k}} times across the window? To answer it, the DFT compares the signal against that wave, sample by sample: multiply them together and add everything up. Where the signal moves in step with the reference wave the products pile up; where it doesn't, they cancel. alias.title: Aliasing: when sampling lies
alias.intro: Everything above rests on one quiet assumption: that N samples are enough to know which wave produced them. This demo is where the assumption breaks. A computer cannot store a smooth curve, only samples of it — here a sine with a frequency you control, sampled at the same 64 evenly spaced points (green dots) no matter how fast it oscillates. To capture a wiggle you need at least 2 samples per cycle: one near a crest, one near a trough. With 64 samples that caps honest measurement at 32 cycles per window. Push beyond it and the samples do not go blank — they lie.

alias.verdictNyquist: {{k}} cycles is exactly N/2. A sine at this frequency crosses zero at every single sample point — all 64 measurements read 0, and the wave vanishes without a trace.
alias.verdictFaithful: {{k}} cycles stays at or below N/2 = 32, so every cycle gets at least 2 samples. The measurements describe the wave truthfully, and the energy lands in bin {{bin}}. The two curves are one and the same.

alias.foldTitle: The folding map — where every true frequency ends up
alias.foldNote: Frequencies fold back and forth like an accordion: up to Nyquist they map to themselves, from 32 to 64 they come back mirrored, past 64 the pattern repeats. The marker is the slider's current position.
alias.whyNote: Why this matters. Between the dots the two curves disagree completely, but sampling never looks between the dots, so no algorithm can recover which wave was real: the evidence is destroyed at the moment of sampling, not by the FFT. That has a physical picture — film a wheel spinning 60 times a second with a 64-frames-per-second camera and it appears to roll slowly backwards, which is why helicopter rotors do impossible things on video. It also has an engineering consequence: since no computation can undo aliasing, real systems prevent it before sampling, with an analog filter that deletes everything above Nyquist. That is why 44.1 kHz audio can only represent tones up to about 22 kHz, and why every analog-to-digital converter ships with an anti-aliasing filter in front of it.
